#1351. JEFF POWELL MBE: I witnessed the unstoppable rot that caused Man United's last relegation - now the ghosts are resurfacing in alarmingly similar fashion for Michael Carrick and his rag-bag of players

By JEFF POWELL MBE, SPORTS WRITER AND BOXING COLUMNIST

Published: 12:02 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 14:02 EDT, 2 November 2026

What more spooky time of the year for a fog of deja vu to be hanging over the haunted house of Old Trafford.

The ghosts of Halloween half a century past have materialised to foretell the doom of relegation.

The omens of 1974 are rewritten in the statistics cursing the current Manchester United team. No win in the first seven away games. A manager without a victory in nine consecutive matches. Perhaps coming up next, a run of only four wins in 20 league matches to match that of the relegation season 52 years ago.

And so to Gloomy Tuesday. If United fail to defeat Roma in the Champions League, they will equal their worst sequence of results in 75 years. The ominous portent for this one is much more recent. If they could lose 4-1 to lowly Como the other week, what chance of beating a major Italian club, unbeaten so far this season in Serie A? With this rag-bag of players, not much.

United’s class of ’74 included England’s Alex Stepney, David Sadler and Brian Kidd, Scotland stars Martin Buchan, George Graham, Lou Macari, Jim McCalliog and Willie Morgan. Graham recalls: ‘The club was going through a difficult time but we did our best.’

Of the team which self-destructed in defeat at Chelsea this Saturday, that could only be truly said of one man. Harry Maguire has survived more criticism than he ever deserved and once again he was alone in looking like he objected to losing.

Denis Law (second right), then of Manchester City, condemns his old club United to relegation in 1974

Following the 2-0 loss at Chelsea on Saturday, if United fail to defeat Roma in the Champions League on Tuesday they will equal their worst sequence of results in 75 years

One of his team-mates, the typically disgraceful Argentine Lisandro Martinez, made sure of defeat by getting himself sent off. Whether that act was deliberate only he can tell us but he looked as anxious to depart this great though ailing club as he had sounded when he criticised its executives after the Como loss.

As did the so-called captain. I voted for Bruno Fernandes as the Footballer of Last Year. Never again. By adding his voice to that of Martinez, he cheapened this great club in its hour of need. That he tried to recant relegates him to the same league of hypocritical back-trackers as Andy Burnham.

The damage to an already badly wounded Michael Carrick has been done. It became irreparable when he agreed to make the peace.

Sir Alex Ferguson would never have forgiven such a breach of trust. But then we are comparing pears with apples here. Fergie is a genius. Carrick simply an honest man out of his depth.

The unfavourable comparisons with the relegation of yesteryear don’t end there. Fernandes is a talented footballer but the idol of ‘74 was another genius.

George Best electrified not only Old Trafford but the world of football and beyond. Champions League glory, two English league titles, Wembley Cup finals, heroic if inevitably hopeless World Cup brilliance with Northern Ireland and a Ballon d’Or would have only been for starters had he not succumbed to his lust for booze and blondes which not only terminated his career but shortened his star-spangled but ultimately tragic life.

Bruno may become remembered as a footnote to Eusebio and Ronaldo in Portugal’s hall of fame. Besty will shine forever in the pantheon of football’s all-time greats.

Best knew when it was the right, self-destructed time to leave. Having torn himself away from Old Trafford in the summer of ’73 he allowed himself to be talked back by the retired Busby.

George Best (left) knew when it was the right time to leave. Having torn himself away from Old Trafford in 1973 he allowed himself to be talked back by the retired Matt Busby (right)

The damage to an already badly wounded Michael Carrick has been done. It became irreparable when he agreed to make peace with the players who spoke out against the club

After a dozen games he accepted that his best would no longer be electrifying enough to spark salvation and after an away defeat on New Year’s Day he said his last goodbye.

As sharp between the ears, surprisingly to some, as he was undeniably mesmerising on the pitch, he left behind words of wisdom gleaned from watching as boy and man as United fell into the turmoil of finding a manager to succeed Sir Matt.

They are as relevant in this time of crisis as they were those 52 years ago: ‘The fear of relegation starts in the boardroom, comes down to the managers and through to the players. The fans sense it.’

The faithful are, indeed, well aware of the origin of the rot besetting the Reds today. They detest the Glazers who brought their American opportunism and apparent greed to Manchester and have plunged the club into billions of debt. They are disenchanted already with Sir Jim Ratcliffe.

Not least because this penny-pinching Englishman’s cost-cutting has broken the hearts of so many loyal servants by sacking them from jobs they loved as much as they do their team. No matter how badly it is playing just now. And, by the way, he can stick his big-top circus stadium in the proverbial orifice.

Manchester United, like Liverpool, belong to the people. Not some damn Yankees and an English fat cat.

Unless this one reclaims its heart, soul, very reason for existing – and damn quickly – the ruin may take decades to rebuild. If ever.

United were heading this way when they were running mindlessly through managers in the 70s and 80s – Dave Sexton was sacked after finishing second in the league for heaven’s sake – until they got lucky as Sir Matt came briefly out of retirement to find his own successor in Sir Alex.

Manchester United, like Liverpool, belong to the people. Not some damn Yankees and an English fat cat in Jim Ratcliffe (centre)

Alex Ferguson (centre, flanked by director Mike Edelson and chairman Martin Edwards) at his unveiling as United boss in 1986, thanks to the help of Busby

The next Greatest Of All Time may never be out there. Carrick accepts it’s not him but the sympathies of the Red Army for a good man doing his darndest for a club he loves as much as they do may keep him going long enough for the increasingly fearful men in the boardroom to make a proper, lasting appointment rather than yet another shot in the dark.

For this they need to take sensible advice from more experienced football men. Just as they must set aside their misguided belief that they know something about the game itself and let seasoned judges guide them towards the really, really best players in which to invest their millions.

Rather than the rabble among the present first team of whose names neither they, nor more importantly the Stretford End, had ever heard until they ambled into Old Trafford.

As the money men should know, if you buy cheap you end up having to buy again. If they don’t, they should follow senors Martinez and Fernandes out of the building.

#1349. Kevin Keegan's iconic Hamburg shirt from 1977 Super Cup against Liverpool sells for £84,500 at auction

Published: 13:58 EDT, 2 November 2026 | Updated: 14:10 EDT, 2 November 2026

Kevin Keegan's iconic 1977 European Super Cup shirt has been sold at auction for a jaw-dropping £84,500.

The 1977 European Super Cup was contested between Liverpool, Keegan's former side, and his new club Hamburg. Despite drawing 1-1 in the first leg, Hamburg lost 6-0 in Keegan's first return to Anfield since his signing.

The much-loved legend's No7 shirt formed part of his former Liverpool team-mate Emlyn Hughes' collection. Hughes, who died in 2004, got it in a swap, and it was estimated at around £2,000 to £3,000 by BUDDS auctioneers.

The sky-blue and white adidas shirt features a v-neck style collar and embroidered badge.

The sale comes just months after the football world was plunged into mourning over the death of Keegan, who was regarded as one of the greatest players of his generation.

Keegan began his playing career at Scunthorpe United in 1968, before Bill Shankly signed him for Liverpool. There, he won seven major trophies including three league titles and one European Cup during a six-year spell.

The 1977 European Super Cup was contested between Liverpool, Keegan's former side, and his new club Hamburg

The much-loved legend's No7 shirt formed part of his former Liverpool team-mate Emlyn Hughes' collection

Ever ambitious, Keegan signed for Hamburg in 1977, and it was during his three-year spell in Germany that the 5ft 7in Englishman earned the nickname the 'Mighty Mouse', winning the league title in 1979 and reaching the 1980 European Cup final, where his side were beaten by Nottingham Forest.

It was also at Hamburg that he confirmed his world-class credentials, winning the Ballon d'Or in 1978 and 1979.

The following year he surprisingly joined Southampton before finishing his playing career with Newcastle, where his love affair with the Geordie fans was born during their 1984 promotion-winning campaign.

Keegan made 63 England appearances and captained his country over 30 times, although his only World Cup was an injury-scarred appearance in 1982.

In 1992, Keegan made his first step into management at his former club Newcastle, guiding them into the Premier League and to within touching distance of the 1995-96 title only to miss out to Manchester United.

After leaving St James' Park in January 1997, a brief stint at Fulham followed before he became England manager in 1999, having initially taken on the job following Glenn Hoddle's departure.

Having overseen a disappointing Euro 2000 campaign, Keegan resigned on the back of defeat by Germany at Wembley Stadium, the last match at the national stadium before it was rebuilt.

After his death, an extraordinary sea of flowers surrounded St James' Park to pay tribute to 'The Messiah' who led their charge back into the top-flight in 1984

After England, he managed Manchester City for four years before returning for a brief spell at Newcastle.

Following his death, an extraordinary sea of flowers surrounded St James' Park to pay tribute to 'The Messiah'.

The club wrote a moving statement at the time, which read: 'We are devastated to learn of the passing of Kevin Keegan, one of the most iconic, influential and deeply loved figures in our club's history.

'Kevin was more than a legendary footballer and manager. He was the beating heart of Newcastle United for generations of supporters.'

#1348. Rio Ngumoha dazzles on coming-of-age night in Europe

There will be many more Champions League nights for Rio Ngumoha, although the 18-year-old will always remember this career landmark when his teenage skill plunged the opposition into fearful indecision and decided the game.

This young man has not yet played 40 senior games but there is no doubting the quality. Alexis Mac Allister scored twice, Liverpool came from two goals behind, and it all ended with a panic that meant they came close to chucking it away again. But what everyone could agree on from this strange match of fluctuating fortunes was that Ngumoha looks like one of the best young players in Europe. He is also a bona fide two-sided winger, winning this game for Liverpool from the right wing rather than his conventional left-wing role.

Ngumoha created the second Liverpool goal for Ronald Araújo and then the third for Mac Allister with the game’s best moment. That was an electrifying run into a group of converging yellow shirts in which he beat two men and still retained the composure to pick out Mac Allister in the area. Even as the Argentine ran to the Kop to celebrate, that stand was chanting the name of the teenager from east London. Ngumoha was one of three academy boys in Andoni Iraola’s XI, along with Lewis Koumas and Trey Nyoni, and all had an impact.

Magic from Rio Ngumoha 🤩🪄 Alexis Mac Allister puts Liverpool ahead with his second goal of the night ⚽️ https://t.co/3FTNWOUYhl

Iraola noted later that Ngumoha had taken care of the defensive work too against Sergi Cardona, an attacking left-back who scored his team’s second goal. From an attacking point of view, Iraola agreed, Ngumoha had periods of the game when he looked unstoppable. “If we can put Rio in situations one-v-one, he makes plays, [and] he produces things,” Iraola said. “The assist for Alexis is a lovely play. He could go down for a penalty but he decides to continue which is a great decision. Also endurance-wise he is able to play more minutes.”

He becomes the youngest Liverpool player in Champions League history to register an assist in the competition. For Iraola it will be hard to leave Ngumoha out of the game against in-form Brighton and Hove Albion on Sunday. “I believe in myself to do it,” Ngumoha said to Amazon Prime TV. “The more chances we get, the more it makes the opposition worry. I just keep going and be ruthless.”

Iraola would later bring on the three £100m attackers whom he had left on the bench, with Sunday’s game in mind. Florian Wirtz, a half-time arrival, scored the fourth and Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak would later come on. Hard to call how it might go at home to Brighton. Liverpool’s defending was erratic at times, but their comeback was impressive.

The floodgates are opening ⚽️ Florian Wirtz scores his first goal of the season for Liverpool 🇩🇪 https://t.co/5HP72tA3bE

Iraola made major changes at half-time, substituting Araújo and playing without a conventional right-back for the second half. It was brave and changed the momentum of the game, pushing his team higher up the pitch in what looked like a man-to-man marking arrangement. It enabled Iraola’s players to deny Villarreal the space and possession they had enjoyed in the first half when they had taken a two-goal lead – chiefly because of the mistakes of the home team. However much that was destabilising for Liverpool, by half-time they were level.

“They are so good on the ball,” Iraola said of Villarreal afterwards. Indeed, Villarreal’s manager Iñigo Pérez, a former Athletic team-mate of the Liverpool manager, was a coach whom Iraola sought to appoint at Bournemouth. “People probably don’t rate them [Villarreal],” Iraola said, “but after Barça they are probably the best in La Liga. They have 61 per cent of possession. Probably they have not had the results they deserve. If you are not really aggressive, you are not going to get the ball.

“We didn’t take as much risk. We were struggling because it is not a team that you can just press a bit. Either you go all the way or you will struggle without the ball.” Once Liverpool had done so, he said, his team had “won a lot of duels”. He was right in that respect. With the space squeezed, it was the power of Liverpool’s midfield that was telling.

Virgil van Dijk gave the first goal to Villarreal’s small No 9 Georges Mikautadze who had looked up to that point like he was hopelessly mismatched against the Liverpool captain and Jérémy Jacquet. Van Dijk’s misjudged header back to Alisson let in the striker, who did well to gather the ball and then hit it early. The second Villarreal goal at the midpoint of the first half was a mistake from Kostas Tsimikas, who failed to step up and played both Mikautadze and Cardona onside from Nathan Saliba’s ball. Either might have tucked it in but it was the left-back Cardona who took it on.

A moment to forget for Virgil van Dijk 😨 Georges Mikautadze takes full advantage to give Villarreal the lead at Anfield 🟡⚽️ https://t.co/3JTl00UwYa

The pace of the game was slow and Villarreal were in control until the later stages of the half. Koumas and Cody Gakpo created a chance and from the corner that resulted Mac Allister headed in Tsimikas’s cross. Liverpool were up and running. Ngumoha’s cross from the left was unwisely left by Cardona for Araújo to score and the game was level.

Out of nowhere 😳 Ronald Araújo sneaks in to grab Liverpool's equaliser on the stroke of half-time 🇺🇾 https://t.co/Qrn8PmB2bJ

Then came Ngumoha’s big second half, creating the third for Mac Allister. The teenager went past Cardona and the substitute Juan Foyth in a couple of strides. Wirtz dispatched the fourth from Gakpo’s ball.

Even so there was still time for Liverpool to show that they had sacrificed some defensive stability. The absence of a right-back cost them when substitute Tani Oluwaseyi ran into that area of the pitch to score Villarreal’s third late on. The third win of Liverpool’s Champions League season puts them second in the 36-team super-table, and behind defending champions Paris St-Germain only on goal difference.

Liverpool are also seeing a new star emerge. Ngumoha might be the most expensive academy signing in the game’s modern history but alongside the £100m men he looks like a risk that was worth taking.

We have said all night about momentum, and talking about how they Liverpool will play against Brighton at the weekend, I’ll be amazed if Rio [Ngumoha] doesn’t start because of the momentum that he has got from this game.

You see the fans, you see how everyone got a lift by him and that’s what they need at the weekend, they need someone to lift them.

They are flying. Their confidence is through the roof. A similar style to Villarreal. They are second in everything after Barcelona. It has been a good game to prepare and we will use it.

I am really happy with Rio. He is trying to improve everything and we are trying to correct things. He played a lot on the left and know he is playing a lot on the right and he has adapted really well. We encourage him always. Even defensively as well he is improving. He has become a more complete player – and we must not forget he is 18!

Rio Ngumoha was magnificent tonight. Such a threat, and he dedicated himself to his tasks. On the ball this kid has so much potential, and I say kid, but he’s a young man. He has so much quality and it’s stuff that you can’t teach to be honest.

What he does with the ball at his feet, that is God given ability, and his hard work on the training pitch, doing things day in and day out, and being ruthless, is what he said in his interview, and I like that. He wants to be decisive, and I love that about him.

I’m not tall but I love going in the box. I really like it. They know I like to attack the near post. I scored in the World Cup as well. It was a good header. The second goal, Rio, was amazing. I talk with him about cutting it back on the floor.

It’s not something I really practice. My dad is a bit smaller than me but he was quite good in the air so maybe it’s something I got from him.

Last year was a really difficult year for all of us. It was clear I was not at the level and I am the first one to say. Something wasn’t right in the group and this manager changed it. The way we play is different, I don’t like to compare. I’m feeling good.

A lot of things happened today. They were much better than us in the first half and we were much better in the second half. When we’ve been under pressure, we answered well. When we relaxed, we made mistakes. You cannot relax against very good opposition. I value the win.

We have to know that if we don’t go to the limit, it will be difficult. We are facing very good teams. It’s good to come back but we’ve started losing too many goals this season.

PSG’s 4-2 win over Barcelona tonight also puts them on nine points. Aston Villa, Arsenal, Real Madrid, Sporting and Real Betis are the teams playing tomorrow night with the opportunity to maintain a 100 per cent record.

Nine points from a possible nine for Liverpool in the Champions League, but they made hard work of it. Some dysfunction was probably to be expected after Iraola decided to start without Mac Allister, Isak, Wirtz and Barcola, but their defensive structure was unzipped far too easily at times.

On the other hand, they dragged themselves off the canvas and the night belonged to Rio Ngumoha. He looked dangerous every time he received the ball, set up the third goal, and received a standing ovation when he was substituted. Liverpool need to put that contract in front of him sharpish.

Still time for another hairy moment at the back for Liverpool, but Perez’ shot from the edge of the area is blocked and that will surely be that.

Pape Gueye floats a cross straight down the throat of Alisson. A wasted opportunity for Villarreal. But still a couple of minutes to play.

Just the three minutes of added time to play, and Liverpool are probably grateful for that.

Could Liverpool be in for a nervous finish? Their defence is caught square again after a run in behind from Ayoze Perez, and Oluwaseyi was totally unmarked at the back post to apply a simple finish at silence Anfield.

Cody Gakpo threatens to score Liverpool’s fifth with an overhead free-kick, teed up by McConnell’s chipped cross to the back post, but he could not keep the attempt down.

The game is meandering towards its conclusion now, though a Villarreal goal would make things interesting.

Another Liverpool youngster enjoys a taste of first-team actions: James McConnell is on for Nyoni.

Liverpool far too easy to play through at the moment, Villarreal might not be an elite team but they have enough technique to pass and move well if given the time. Better from Liverpool with Nyoni driving forward and the ball almost running into the path of Gravenberch for a strike from the edge of the box. Villarreal diligent in their defensive work though, no clear sight of goal for the Liverpool players so far.

Anyone who is experiencing Anfield on a European night for the first time will be wondering what all the fuss is about. Aside from a couple of flurries following a Ronald Araujo tackle and a Rio Ngumoha dribble, it has been deathly quiet. Rafael Benitez, an architect of some of the wildest evenings here, is in the press box alongside Robbie Fowler and they are a reminder of how it used to be. Liverpool need to raise themselves to bring the crowd to life.

Ngumoha is the one ray of light for Liverpool so far, he has the beating of Villarreal left-back Cardona whenever he drops a shoulder. Gulasci palms his deflected cross over and Villarreal survive the corner.

The flag was eventually raised for offside, but Villarreal were in behind the Liverpool defence again after a misplaced Van Dijk pass. Liverpool have not got themselves out of the blocks at all. They have lost possession too cheaply and look vulnerable defensively.

Buchanan with a teasing low cross through the Liverpool penalty area, and the winger is justified when looking quizzically at his team-mates. If one of the yellow shirts had gambled they would have had a tap in.

Most of Liverpool’s attacks are being funnelled down their right so far, perhaps no surprise given that is where Ngumoha is stationed. Liverpool yet to test the goalkeeper, though.

Villarreal then throw a punch of their own down the other end, with Saliba turning and shooting at the edge of the box. Deflected, and Villarreal have a corner. Delivery is poor and Liverpool clear.

The Spanish team are moving the ball around with assurance, some nice touches from Saliba in their midfield (the Canada international is no relation to the Arsenal centre-back).

Hats off to Villarreal coach Inigo Perez, who is not wearing a hat or, indeed, a coat. Instead he is steadfastly ignoring the cold drizzle and treating this, from a touchline outfit point of view, like a warm summer’s evening on the Valencian coast. Polo shirt and slacks for the young Spanish coach.

No need for Liverpool to panic just yet, plenty of time to turn this around, and Rio Ngumoha is going the right way about it. Quick feet in the box to beat his man and fashion a yard for a strike, but his shot is blocked. Ngumoha is playing on Liverpool’s right tonight with Gakpo on the opposite flank.

What a remarkable start. Virgil van Dijk has looked a gear or two behind everyone in the opening stages. One bad touch required Jeremy Jacquet to make a swift recovery and that misplaced header has now handed Villarreal the lead. Social media will be abuzz with scrutiny about Van Dijk now, as is always the case when he errs, but it won’t be taken into consideration that he has been one of Liverpool’s best players in these opening 10 games. What price would you make him to atone with a header at the other end later in the game?

Van Dijk has made two dreadful mistakes in the first four minutes and this time he is punished. Liverpool’s captain was trying to guide a header back to Alisson, but the ball shanked off his forehead at the wrong angle and dropped for Mikautadze in the box. The striker was free, and he finished well across Alisson. That was not in the script.

The Georgian No 9 for Villarreal Georges Mikautadze had looked so lightweight in the early duels with Virgil Van Dijk and Jeremy Jacquet. They had muscled him off the ball more than once. That was a gift from Van Dijk and Mikautadze took it very well.

A very interesting team selection from Andoni Iraola. Liverpool’s head coach had indicated at his pre-match press conference that he was going to go as strong as possible, as his side seek to secure their third straight Champions League win. But the very fact Iraola has chosen to put Florian Wirtz and Bradley Barcola on the bench indicates he has one eye on Sunday’s demanding assignment against Brighton at Anfield.

Iraola will be delighted to have Cody Gakpo fit again and Lewis Koumas certainly deserves another opportunity to lead the line. But after victory’s against Atletico Madrid and LASK, Liverpool have given themselves some breathing space and it is understandable if Iraola, who has bemoaned the lack of time he has to train his squad, is already plotting Brighton’s downfall.

Your Reds to take on Villarreal in the #UCL! 🔴💫 https://t.co/tlQNFZVMBv

The club known as the “Yellow Submarine” made themselves some fans in the red half of Merseyside by denying Everton a place in the Champions League proper in 2005/06. Everton lost 4-2 on aggregate, and there was controversy in the second leg in Spain when Pierluigi Collina disallowed a Duncan Ferguson header that could have taken the tie to extra time. Everton had finished fourth, one place above Liverpool, the previous season, but Liverpool’s triumph in Istanbul assured them of a qualification place too. Unlike Everton, they prevailed.

Speaking of which, Rafael Benitez is at Anfield this evening.

Dominic King takes stock of Andoni Iraola’s first 10 games in charge of Liverpool and, despite some teething problems, he believes there are reasons to be optimistic. The demands Iraola is putting on Liverpool’s midfielders are an interesting tactical wrinkle, with Dom writing: “Liverpool’s formation will always be written as 4-2-3-1, but the reality is that Iraola’s team do not play in four clear tactical lines. He asks specific jobs of his midfielders, deploying them detailed instructions, and it is going to require some patience before performances become consistent.”

A precious victory at Brentford, Bradley Barcola and Alexander Isak among the goals and a couple of improved showings from Florian Wirtz mean things now look a little brighter for Liverpool.

They are strong favourites to make it nine points from nine in the Champions League by beating Villarreal at Anfield this evening, the Spanish club they vanquished in the 2022 semi-finals under Jürgen Klopp.

Liverpool drew Atletico Madrid at home (already ticked off) and Inter Milan away as their two pot-one fixtures, which is about as kind as you can expect. A top-two finish in the league phase is a realistic aspiration for Andoni Iraola’s team, and something would need to go badly awry for them to miss out on the top eight.

Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Isak returned from injury to strengthen Liverpool at Brentford, although Szoboszlai has been lost for a few weeks following another hamstring complication.

Villarreal have punched well above their weight in Europe for the past few decades, reaching two European Cup semi-finals (beaten by Arsenal in 2006 as well as Liverpool in 2022) and winning the Europa League under Unai Emery in 2021.

They have been mediocre in La Liga so far this season though, 12th after nine games on nine points and with a goal difference of zero. Their Champions League performances have been promising though, losing by the odd goal in a frantic finish at Borussia Dortmund and beating Napoli 3-1 at home. Villarreal’s best player is probably Senegalese central midfielder Pape Gueye, and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pépé is also in their ranks. Gueye, despite his position, is their joint-top scorer in all competitions with three goals.

Iraola will be up against his close friend and former Athletic Bilbao team-mate Inigo Perez who is now in charge at Villarreal. Perez was also Iraola’s assistant at Rayo Vallecano, the job which earned the Basque his move to Bournemouth. Perez guided Rayo Vallecano to the Uefa Conference League final last season.

#1347. Presynaptic homeostasis mediated by exocytosis of a SNARE protein

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The neural plasticity that underlies adaptation and learning requires countervailing homeostatic mechanisms to maintain the stability and responsiveness of neural circuits. Previous work has described several forms of synaptic homeostasis1, but the mechanisms that detect changes in activity and transduce these into altered neurotransmission have remained poorly understood. Here we show that high-frequency stimulation alters the subsequent properties of neurotransmitter release to confer a presynaptic form of homeostasis, independent of postsynaptic receptors. The mechanism involves vesicular SNARE protein (v-SNARE) VAMP7 (vesicle-associated membrane protein 7), which reduces neurotransmitter release by inhibiting the entry of Ca2+ specifically through P/Q-type presynaptic Ca2+ channels. Previous work has implicated target SNARE proteins (t-SNAREs) in the inhibition of Ca2+ channels2, but without clear physiological rationale. We show that the activity-dependent regulation of release mediated by VAMP7 requires the t-SNARE syntaxin. Although VAMP7 acts at the plasma membrane to inhibit P/Q-type channels, it localizes predominantly to a subset of synaptic vesicles made by adaptor protein-3 (AP-3) that respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3,4. The localization of VAMP7 to AP-3-derived synaptic vesicles thus provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it associates with syntaxin to inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels and transmitter release. This homeostatic form of metaplasticity operates at multiple excitatory synapses, and in its absence, the fraction of FOS+ neurons increases several fold, revealing a general property of excitatory neurotransmission that might also maintain the sparsity of neural connections.

Homeostatic synaptic plasticity can involve pre- or postsynaptic mechanisms. In response to a global change in activity, mammalian central neurons alter the expression of glutamate receptors1,5,6,7. By contrast, a presynaptic form of homeostasis occurs at the neuromuscular junction. First established in Drosophila melanogaster, this involves increased release of glutamate in response to reduced postsynaptic receptor function8,9. An effect of activity on neurotransmitter release has also been reported at central synapses10,11,12,13,14,15,16,17,18. Although previous work has identified several elements that are required for the different forms of homeostatic plasticity, the mechanisms involved remain poorly understood.

To determine the time course over which presynaptic homeostatic plasticity develops, we suppressed network activity by treating primary mouse hippocampal cultures, which contain almost entirely glutamatergic neurons (Extended Data Fig. 1a,b), with the glutamate receptor antagonists 6-cyano-7-nitroquinoxaline-2,3-dione (CNQX) and 3-(2-carboxypiperazin-4-yl)propyl-1-phosphonic acid (commonly known as APV). We monitored the consequent changes in transmitter release using a fusion of the strongly pH-sensitive GFP variant ecliptic pHluorin to a luminal loop of the vesicular glutamate transporter VGLUT1 (VGLUT1–pH). Quenched at the low pH of synaptic vesicles (SVs), the pHluorin-based reporter brightens on exposure to the higher external pH at exocytosis; the reacidification that accompanies endocytosis results in requenching. Figure 1a,b shows that silencing with CNQX and APV increases both the rate and the extent of VGLUT1+ SV exocytosis. The reacidification that accompanies endocytosis also slows (Fig. 1a,b), but stimulation in the presence of the v-type H+-ATPase inhibitor bafilomycin to block SV reacidification results in an increase in the proportion of VGLUT1+ SVs available for release, independent of any change in endocytosis16 (Fig. 1c). We detect no change in the punctate distribution of SVs or the active zone (Extended Data Fig. 1c). To assess the initial release probability, we monitored glutamate release at individual presynaptic boutons using the glutamate sensor iGluSnFR (ref. 19). Stimulating at a low frequency (0.2 Hz), we find that silencing the cultures increases the proportion of synapses that release glutamate (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1d). Because a change in release probability can reflect a change in the presynaptic Ca2+ entry that triggers release, we monitored presynaptic Ca2+ with the low-affinity Ca2+ dye Fluo5F. Figure 1e,f shows that silencing the cultures greatly increases the presynaptic Ca2+ response to both 5-Hz and 25-Hz stimulus trains. This large increase in Ca2+ entry might be expected to increase the release probability more than the doubling that was observed, but we used iGluSnFR only to indicate whether release occurred, and this binary measure underestimates the actual increase in release probability. In addition, stimulation at 1 Hz and 5 Hz triggers Ca2+ entry with near 100% reliability in all presynaptic boutons (Extended Data Fig. 2). Thus, silencing cannot increase the proportion of responsive boutons, excluding effects on action potential invasion of the nerve terminal. Ongoing neural activity thus seems to reduce glutamate release by suppressing presynaptic Ca2+ entry.

a, Wild-type (WT) hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were treated with CNQX (10 μM) and APV (50 μM) for the times indicated and stimulated at 25 Hz for 20 s. The fluorescence response normalized to total fluorescence was revealed in 50 mM NH4Cl. b, Left, peak response and initial rate (first 4 s) of fluorescence increase. Right, time constant (τ) of endocytosis (0 h and 24 h, n = 20/3 (see end of legend for explanation of n numbers); 3 h, n = 14/3; 6 h and 48 h, n = 16/3). c, WT hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were silenced for 24 h, stimulated at 25 Hz for 120 s in the presence of 100 nM bafilomycin A1 (Baf) and the response was normalized as above. Scatter plots show exocytosis rate and recycling pool size (control, n = 14/3; CNQX + APV, n = 16/3). d, WT hippocampal neurons expressing iGluSnFR–stargazin were silenced for 24 h and stimulated 30 times at 0.2 Hz to measure the release probability (Pr). Pr is shown as a cumulative frequency distribution and as a box-and-whisker plot, with centre line indicating the median, box bounds 25th−75th percentiles and whiskers minimum and maximum values (n = 12/3). e,f,h, WT hippocampal neurons silenced with CNQX + APV (e,f) or 1 μM TTX (h) for 24 h and loaded with Fluo5F were stimulated at 5 Hz for 5 s (e) (control, n = 16/3; CNQX + APV, n = 18/3) or stimulated repeatedly at 25 Hz for 5 s each, with 15 s between bursts and fluorescence normalized to baseline (f,h) (f, control, n = 14/3; CNQX + APV, n = 20/3; h, n = 10/2, both conditions). AUC, area under the curve. g,i, WT hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH and silenced with CNQX + APV (g) or TTX (i) for 24 h were stimulated twice at 25 Hz for 20 s and the response was normalized as above. Scatter plots show the slope of fluorescence increase and the fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (g, control, n = 11/3; CNQX + APV, n = 10/3; i, n = 14/3, both conditions). Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = x/y, where x indicates the fields examined and y the number of independent experiments. Significance by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (c–e), one-way (b) or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (f–i).

To determine whether activity can reverse the effects of silencing, we stimulated the neurons with repeated 25-Hz bursts. We find that two to three bursts reduces the Ca2+ entry in silenced neurons back to baseline, with no effect on presynaptic Ca2+ entry in unsilenced cultures (Fig. 1f). To assess the effects on release, we imaged VGLUT1–pH. Stimulation at 25 Hz also reverses the increased rate and extent of release due to silencing, with no effect on the unsilenced neurons (Fig. 1g). Thus, activity can acutely reverse the homeostatic increase in transmitter release. Stimulation reverses the effects of silencing despite the continued presence of glutamate receptor antagonists, indicating that the mechanism does not require the activation of postsynaptic receptors and is thus induced presynaptically. Silencing with tetrodotoxin (TTX) for 24 h similarly enhances presynaptic Ca2+ entry and transmitter release that reverses rapidly with repeated 25-Hz stimulation (in the absence of TTX) (Fig. 1h,i), supporting the role of neural activity, rather than being a phenomenon restricted to the inactivation of glutamate receptors.

To determine whether activity suppresses release in a more physiological preparation, we extended the analysis to Schaffer-collateral synapses in the stratum radiatum of CA1 hippocampus. We compared the effect of 100 action potentials (APs) delivered at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz (followed by a 20-s gap to allow some recovery) on the response to test stimulation at 5 Hz. With intervening stimulation at 5 Hz, the final stimulus train shows incomplete recovery of the first response but synaptic depression similar to that observed with the first train (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a), indicating that the properties of release have not changed. Despite delivering the same number of APs, intervening stimulation at 50 Hz increases facilitation and reduces subsequent synaptic depression (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 3a). This suggests a reduction in the initial release probability that enables the accumulation of Ca2+ without depleting SVs20—a fundamental change in the properties of release.

a–e, Left, sample traces from CA1 stratum radiatum showing the effects of 100 stimuli (blue), delivered at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz, on test stimulation (also 100 AP) delivered before (black) and after (red) at 5 Hz in hippocampal slices from WT (a,b), mocha (c), Atp8a1-KO (d) and Vamp7-KO (e) mice. Hatched lines indicate a gap of 20 s. Middle, response to each stimulus normalized to the first response. Right, response of different cells to action potential 2 (AP2) (b–e) and AP95 (a–e), normalized by the response to AP1 (a, n = 17/3; b,c, n = 21/3; d,e, n = 22/3). EPSC, excitatory postsynaptic current. f, After incubation for 10 min in the presence of MK-801, CA1 pyramidal neurons were held at −70 mV and Schaffer-collateral inputs were stimulated at 0 Hz, 5 Hz or 50 Hz (100 AP). Twenty seconds after this stimulation (the hatched lines), cells were held at +40 mV and NMDAR-EPSCs were elicited at 0.2 Hz. Graphs show progressive MK-801 inhibition normalized to the first response and the corresponding decay time constants (τ) in WT and Vamp7-KO slices (n = 13/3). g, WT and Vamp7-KO hippocampal neurons expressing VGLUT1–pH were silenced with CNQX + APV for 24 h, stimulated at 5 Hz or 25 Hz for 20 s and the response normalized as above. Scatter plots (right) show fluorescence at the end of the stimulus (n = 16/3). Data are mean ± s.e.m.; n = x/y, where x indicates the cell or field number and y the number of independent experiments. Significance by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test (a–f) or two-way ANOVA with Tukey’s multiple-comparisons test (g).

We wanted to understand how high-frequency stimulation suppresses subsequent transmitter release. Previous work has shown that the heterotetrameric adaptor protein AP-3 produces a subset of SVs from endosomes21,22, distinct from the production of canonical SVs at the plasma membrane (or immediately after endocytosis) by clathrin and the related adaptor AP-2 (refs. 23,24,25). We previously found that loss of AP-3 impairs release specifically to stimulation at a high frequency3,4. Thus, we investigated whether loss of AP-3 impairs the suppression of release that follows high-frequency stimulation. Slices from mocha mice, which lack AP-3, show increased rather than reduced synaptic depression after 50-Hz stimulation (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3b). Consistent with the role of AP-3 in producing SVs that are responsive specifically to strong stimulation (that is, of low release probability), AP-3 is thus required for the suppression of release after high-frequency stimulation, and previous work has shown that loss of AP-3 has little effect on response to the 5-Hz test stimulation itself3.

The dependence on AP-3 predicted that a specific component of SVs made by this adaptor is responsible for the suppression of release after strong stimulation. Indeed, a small subset of SV proteins depend on AP-3 for targeting to SVs. These include the zinc transporter ZnT3 (ref. 26), the phospholipid flippase ATP8A1 (ref. 3) and the endolysosomal v-SNARE (vesicular soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) VAMP7 (refs. 27,28). Because a zinc transporter seemed to be more likely to influence postsynaptic glutamate receptors29 than to affect release, we focused on the two other proteins. Although enriched in mossy-fibre terminals, ATP8A1 and VAMP7 are highly expressed throughout the hippocampus, including in CA1 and CA3, and localize to SVs30 (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). Single-cell RNA-sequencing analysis indicates that both genes are expressed in CA3 pyramidal neurons31 (Extended Data Fig. 4c). Western blot analysis confirms the enrichment of both proteins in SVs from the stratum radiatum and stratum lacunosum-moleculare (Extended Data Fig. 4d). In hippocampal slices from Atp8a1-knockout (KO) mice, 50-Hz stimulation still reduces subsequent synaptic depression in the CA1 stratum radiatum (Fig. 2d and Extended Data Fig. 3c). However, loss of VAMP7 (Vamp7 KO) increases synaptic depression, and 50-Hz stimulation does not alter the increased depression (Fig. 2e and Extended Data Fig. 3d). Loss of VAMP7 thus seems to account for the role of AP-3 in the effect of high-frequency activity on subsequent release.

Differences in synaptic depression might result from differential recruitment of Schaffer-collateral input, but varying the stimulus intensity threefold does not affect the kinetics or the extent of short-term depression with 5-Hz stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 3e). The effect also persists under more physiological recording conditions (1.5 mM Ca2+, 1 mM Mg2+), which reduce the initial release probability but still allow 50-Hz stimulation to reduce the subsequent release probability in wild-type (WT) but not in Vamp7-KO slices (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f).

To assess the release probability directly, we took advantage of the use-dependent N-methyl-d-aspartate receptor (NMDAR) antagonist MK-801. Slices pre-incubated in MK-801 were subjected to a conditioning train at either 5 Hz or 50 Hz while the postsynaptic cell was held at −70 mV. Stimulating at 0.2 Hz to assess the ‘initial’ response, NMDAR-EPSCs were then recorded at +40 mV in the continued presence of MK-801. As shown in Fig. 2f, previous 50-Hz stimulation of WT slices slows MK-801 blockade to a greater extent than does previous stimulation at 5 Hz, whereas blockade by MK-801 in Vamp7-KO slices does not change with previous stimulation. Thus, high-frequency stimulation reduces the release probability, and loss of VAMP7 blocks this effect.

VAMP7 is widely expressed throughout the nervous system (Extended Data Fig. 5a). We thus examined three other facilitating synapses: perforant-path synapses formed by layer 2 and 3 neurons of the entorhinal cortex onto dentate granule cells; corticothalamic synapses made by cortical layer 6 pyramidal cells onto ventrobasal thalamic relay neurons; and cerebellar parallel-fibre synapses onto Purkinje cells. Similar to CA1 stratum radiatum, 50-Hz stimulation at each of these synapses reduces synaptic depression (Extended Data Fig. 5b–d). In addition, loss of VAMP7 increases synaptic depression and eliminates the effect of 50-Hz stimulation, supporting a general role for VAMP7 in neurotransmission. Loss of VAMP7 does not affect the presynaptic expression of canonical SNARE proteins in SVs, the punctate distribution of SVs or the active-zone protein Piccolo (Extended Data Fig. 6a,b), suggesting that VAMP7 has a specific effect on release.

If VAMP7 is required for suppression of release after high-frequency stimulation, it should also have a key role in the increase in release due to silencing. We thus used VGLUT1–pH to monitor SV exocytosis. In unsilenced cultures, loss of VAMP7 increases SV exocytosis relative to WT across a range of stimulation frequencies (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d). Although silencing with glutamate receptor antagonists increases release from WT neurons, silencing does not further increase release in Vamp7-KO neurons (Fig. 2g). Thus, the increased release observed in the absence of VAMP7 occludes the effect of silencing, suggesting that silencing inactivates VAMP7. Consistent with the hypothesis that VAMP7 has a role in the inhibition of release, overexpression of VAMP7 inhibits the exocytosis of VGLUT1–pH and VGLUT2–pH, particularly at a high frequency (Extended Data Fig. 6c,d).

We next investigated how VAMP7 suppresses release. In hippocampal slices, loss of VAMP7 impairs synaptic facilitation and increases depression with low-frequency stimulation (Fig. 3a,b and Extended Data Fig. 7a), consistent with the results in culture and suggesting an increased initial release probability. Mossy fibres in the hippocampus express high levels of VAMP7 (refs. 28,32), and a recent study33 has investigated the properties of mossy-fibre synapses in the absence of VAMP7. In contrast to our findings in CA1 stratum radiatum, this study found no change in the properties of transmitter release at mossy-fibre synapses33. This might reflect a difference between the two synapses, but the experiments were also performed at room temperature rather than at the 35 °C used here. We thus repeated the analysis of Schaffer-collateral synapses in CA1 stratum radiatum at room temperature, and found that the effect of Vamp7 KO on 5-Hz and 25-Hz stimulus trains disappears (Extended Data Fig. 7b). Vamp7 KO has no effect on the paired-pulse ratio (PPR) at room temperature, but at 34–35 °C it results in a clear reduction in the PPR, consistent with an increased release probability at this more physiological temperature34 (Extended Data Fig. 7c). At 34–35 °C, mossy-fibre synapses show modestly reduced facilitation in the absence of VAMP7 (Extended Data Fig. 7d), consistent with an increase in the release probability at this synapse as well as at Schaffer collaterals. Temperature thus accounts for the discrepant results, and VAMP7 has qualitatively similar effects at both Schaffer-collateral and mossy-fibre synapses.

The analysis of initial release probability after stimulation suggested that loss of VAMP7 increases the release probability (Fig. 2f). A direct comparison of WT and Vamp7-KO slices confirms this observation (Fig. 3c). Because the initial release probability mostly reflects Ca2+ entry, we varied the external Ca2+ concentration and found that 4 mM Ca2+ occludes the effect of Vamp7 KO on release by Schaffer collaterals (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 7e), consistent with an increase in Ca2+ entry owing to the loss of VAMP7. To determine whether loss of VAMP7 affects Ca2+ at individual presynaptic boutons, we used the low-affinity Ca2+ indicator Fluo5F to monitor Ca2+ entry at the boutons of cultured hippocampal neurons labelled with the red-shifted styryl dye FM4-64 (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Figure 3e shows that at all frequencies tested (1–50 Hz), cultured Vamp7-KO neurons exhibit higher evoked Ca2+ transients than do WT cells, and that the low-affinity Fluo5F does not saturate under these conditions (Extended Data Fig. 8b). At a high frequency, Vamp7-KO but not WT neurons progressively accumulate Ca2+, perhaps because an increased Ca2+ load overwhelms the mechanisms for Ca2+ clearance.

To determine whether the effect of VAMP7 on Ca2+ entry extends to other v-SNAREs, we used lentiviral transduction of the light chain of tetanus toxin (TeNT) to cleave the canonical SV SNARE VAMP2 (ref. 35). Despite complete cleavage of VAMP2 (Fig. 3f) and the resulting inhibition of release (Extended Data Fig. 8c), TeNT has no effect on the punctate localization of SV and active-zone proteins (Fig. 3g), and does not alter the presynaptic entry of Ca2+ at a wide range of stimulation frequencies in WT or Vamp7-KO neurons (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Because TeNT also cleaves the related v-SNAREs VAMP1 and VAMP3 but not VAMP7 (ref. 36), the regulation of presynaptic Ca2+ entry by v-SNAREs seems to be unique to the non-canonical v-SNARE VAMP7.

VAMP7 localizes mainly to intracellular membranes, so we wondered how it could suppress presynaptic Ca2+ entry evoked by stimulation. Depolarization of the nerve terminal activates voltage-gated channels to allow Ca2+ entry, but release from intracellular stores might contribute37,38,39. To determine whether VAMP7 inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry across the plasma membrane, we took advantage of a mutation that blocks the endocytosis of VAMP2, trapping it at the cell surface40 (Extended Data Fig. 9a–c). Introducing the equivalent mutation (M140A) into VAMP7–pH disrupts its punctate localization at presynaptic boutons in hippocampal cultures (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 9c), greatly increases the surface fraction, as determined by quenching with cell-impermeant, low-pH buffer (Fig. 3j and Extended Data Fig. 9d), and eliminates the response of VAMP7–pH to stimulation at multiple frequencies (Fig. 3k and Extended Data Fig. 9e). VAMP7(M140A) thus localizes almost exclusively to the plasma membrane. In Vamp7-KO neurons, VAMP7(M140A) reduces presynaptic Ca2+ entry back to the level observed in WT neurons (Fig. 3l) and inhibits SV exocytosis to the same extent that WT VAMP7 does (Extended Data Fig. 9f). Thus, VAMP7 inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry at the plasma membrane.

The presynaptic voltage-gated Ca2+ channels that trigger transmitter release generally belong to the N and P/Q types41. To determine which type is inhibited by VAMP7, we took advantage of neurotoxins that block specific channel types. Figure 3m shows that ω-agatoxin IVA, which targets Cav2.1 (the P/Q/-type voltage-gated calcium channel), greatly reduces the increased presynaptic Ca2+ entry that is triggered at a wide range of stimulation frequencies in cultured Vamp7-KO neurons, including the progressive increase in Ca2+ that is observed with high-frequency stimulation. ω-Agatoxin also inhibits Ca2+ entry in WT neurons, but the extent of inhibition is greater in Vamp7-KO neurons. Consistent with this, previous work has shown that Ca2+ entry specifically through P/Q-type channels changes as a function of neural activity17. By contrast, the N-type Ca2+ channel inhibitor ω-conotoxin GVIA has a more modest effect that is similar in Vamp7-KO and in WT neurons (Fig. 3m and Extended Data Fig. 10a). The L-type Ca2+ channel inhibitor nimodipine and R-type inhibitor SNX-482 have little effect on presynaptic Ca2+ entry in WT neurons, and little effect in Vamp7-KO neurons stimulated at a low frequency (Extended Data Fig. 10b). However, nimodipine substantially reduces Ca2+ entry in Vamp7-KO neurons stimulated at 25 Hz (Extended Data Fig. 10b). Thus, VAMP7 inhibits P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at all frequencies and L-type channels at a high frequency. Because previous work has implicated intracellular Ca2+ stores in transmitter release42,43, we also depleted intracellular Ca2+ using the sarco/endoplasmic reticulum Ca2+-ATPase (SERCA) inhibitor thapsigargin. Thapsigargin reduces Ca2+ entry at low and high frequencies, but loss of VAMP7 has no effect on the extent of inhibition (Extended Data Fig. 10c).

To determine whether the observed effect of VAMP7 on P/Q-type Ca2+ channels accounts for the changes in transmitter release in the Vamp7 KO, we used slice recording. ω-Agatoxin IVA inhibits release (1 AP) to a greater extent in Vamp7-KO slices than it does in WT slices (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e), consistent with the disinhibition of P/Q-type channels. By contrast, ω-conotoxin has the same, small effect in both WT and Vamp7-KO slices, and nimodipine has essentially no effect on the response to single stimuli in either genotype (Extended Data Fig. 10d,e). A change in Ca2+ entry should also influence short-term plasticity. Extended Data Fig. 10e,f shows that ω-agatoxin reduces synaptic depression to a much greater extent in the Vamp7 KO than in the WT, reflecting a greater reduction in release probability. By contrast, ω-conotoxin has little effect in either WT or Vamp7 KO. Thus, loss of VAMP7 increases the reliance on P/Q-type channels specifically for release.

Next, we examined how VAMP7 contributes to the inhibition of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. Previous work has shown that the t-SNAREs syntaxin and SNAP25 interact with N- and P/Q-type Ca2+ channels at a specific (‘synprint’) site between the second and third homology repeats44,45,46. In heterologous expression systems, the t-SNAREs inhibit voltage-gated Ca2+ channels47, but when assembled with synaptotagmin, their disinhibition has been suggested to promote the coupling of release to Ca2+ entry48,49,50. The role of v-SNAREs in this form of regulation has remained unclear. We find that loss of VAMP7 does not alter the punctate distribution of Cav2.1 or Cav2.2, or their colocalization with the SV protein synaptophysin or with the active-zone protein Piccolo (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 11a,b). However, loss of VAMP7 reduces the colocalization of syntaxin 1 with Cav2.1 (Fig. 4b), whereas colocalization with Cav2.2 does not change (Extended Data Fig. 11c). In terms of biochemical interaction, VAMP7 and syntaxin 1 co-immunoprecipitate with P/Q-type channels in synaptosomes from WT mice (Fig. 4c). In membranes from Vamp7-KO mice, however, less syntaxin co-immunoprecipitates with the channel, suggesting that VAMP7 stabilizes the interaction of syntaxin with Cav2.1. By contrast, the association of SNAP25 with the channel does not depend on VAMP7 (Fig. 4c).

To determine whether syntaxin and SNAP25 are required for the effect of VAMP7 on Ca2+ channels, we made use of the clostridial neurotoxins that cleave these t-SNAREs51. Botulinum neurotoxin C (BoNT/C) cleaves syntaxins52, and previous work has shown that it increases Ca2+ entry53,54. Complete loss of syntaxin 1 impairs the development of hippocampal cultures55, so we added the holotoxin one day before imaging, which results in the cleavage of syntaxin 1 without apparent toxicity (Extended Data Fig. 11d,e). BoNT/C increases presynaptic Ca2+ entry in primary neuronal culture stimulated at frequencies from 1 Hz to 50 Hz (Fig. 4d). With 1-AP stimulation, treatment of Vamp7-KO neurons with BoNT/C produces no further increase in Ca2+ entry, and loss of VAMP7 has no additional effect on the increase due to BoNT/C (Fig. 4d), indicating that VAMP7 and syntaxin are both required to inhibit Ca2+ entry triggered by single APs. Consistent with a common mechanism, the increased Ca2+ entry produced by BoNT/C in response to 1-AP stimulation is inhibited by ω-agatoxin IVA, but not by the N- and L-type channel inhibitors, supporting the disinhibition of mainly P/Q-type channels (Fig. 4e). Although BoNT/C also partially cleaves SNAP25 (Extended Data Fig. 11d), complete cleavage of SNAP25 by lentiviral transduction of the more selective BoNT/A light chain54 has minimal effect on Ca2+ entry in WT neurons (Fig. 4f and Extended Data Fig. 12a,b). In the Vamp7 KO, however, BoNT/A increases Ca2+ entry with low-frequency as well as with high-frequency stimulation (Extended Data Fig. 12c). Thus, in contrast to VAMP7 and syntaxin, which are both required to inhibit Ca2+ entry through P/Q-type channels, SNAP25 regulates Ca2+ entry only in the absence of VAMP7.

To understand how VAMP7 and syntaxin contribute to the inhibition of presynaptic Ca2+ channels, we first determined whether the proteins can form a complex. Expressed in HEK293 cells, Strep-tagged Cav2.1 immunoprecipitates VAMP7 when co-expressed with syntaxin 1 and the auxiliary Ca2+ channel subunits β3 and α2δ1 (Fig. 4g). SNAP25 can by itself associate with the channel, but—consistent with the selective effect of BoNT/C but not BoNT/A on Ca2+ entry in WT neurons—syntaxin 1, but not SNAP25, is required for co-immunoprecipitation of VAMP7 by Cav2.1 (Fig. 4g). Deletion of the synprint domain in Cav2.1 eliminates the interaction (Extended Data Fig. 13a). Extending the analysis to cortical neurons, immunoprecipitation of GFP–VAMP7 introduced into the Vamp7 KO pulls down Cav2.1, particularly when syntaxin 1 is also introduced (Extended Data Fig. 13b).

In addition to a SNARE domain, VAMP7 contains several domains not present in VAMP2 that might account for the inhibition of P/Q-type Ca2+ channels. In particular, VAMP7 contains a longin domain, which binds to AP-3 and influences SNARE-complex formation27,56. To test the role of this and other domains, we introduced luminally GFP-tagged WT and mutant VAMP2 and VAMP7 into cortical cultures from the Vamp7 KO. Figure 4h shows that VAMP2 interacts as anticipated with syntaxin and SNAP25 but does not immunoprecipitate endogenous Cav2.1. By contrast, VAMP7 immunoprecipitates Cav2.1 as well as the t-SNAREs, but the longin domain is not required (Fig. 4h). Chimerae of VAMP2 and VAMP7 in the SNARE domain are all sufficient to immunoprecipitate Cav2.1, but removing the linker between the longin and SNARE domains eliminates the interaction with Cav2.1. Consistent with this, replacing the linker in VAMP7 with the VAMP2 linker disrupts the interaction, and replacing the linker in VAMP2 with the VAMP7 linker promotes it, but none of these mutations interferes with the formation of SNARE complexes (Fig. 4h).

If the linker is required for interaction of VAMP7 with Cav2.1, it should also be required for VAMP7 to inhibit Ca2+ entry. Introducing WT and mutant VAMP7 into cultured hippocampal neurons from the Vamp7 KO, we find that deletion of the longin domain does not affect the inhibition of Ca2+ entry by VAMP7 for either 1 AP or 25-Hz stimulation (Fig. 4i and Extended Data Fig. 13c). However, a larger deletion that includes the linker eliminates the inhibition of Ca2+ entry. As shown above for the interaction with Cav2.1, replacing the linker in VAMP7 with the VAMP2 linker also eliminates the inhibition of Ca2+ entry, and replacing the linker in VAMP2 with the VAMP7 linker enables the inhibition (Fig. 4i). Interaction with Cav2.1 might retain VAMP7 at the plasma membrane, but the linker mutant defective in Cav2.1 binding exhibits exo- and endocytosis kinetics indistinguishable from those of the WT (Extended Data Fig. 13d). Thus, the VAMP7 linker is required specifically to bind to and inhibit P/Q-type Ca2+ channels.

Plasma membrane VAMP7 inhibits P/Q-type Ca2+ channels, but VAMP7 localizes predominantly to the subset of SVs made by AP-3. Because AP-3-derived SVs respond specifically to high-frequency stimulation3, we hypothesized that localization of VAMP7 to these SVs provides a mechanism for the activity-dependent delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane, where it inhibits presynaptic Ca2+ entry. This hypothesis makes several predictions. First, strong stimulation should suppress release in a VAMP7-dependent manner. Indeed, repeated stimulation of WT hippocampal neurons at 50 Hz reduces the subsequent exocytic response monitored with VGLUT1–pH (Fig. 5a). Although there are many potential causes, loss of VAMP7 greatly reduces the decline (Fig. 5a), even though the initial response is greater in the absence of VAMP7. Extending the analysis to CA1 hippocampus, repeated 50-Hz bursts progressively reduce synaptic responses in WT slices, and loss of VAMP7 again attenuates the decline (Extended Data Fig. 14a). Loss of AP-3 has a similar but more modest effect because although delivery of VAMP7 to the plasma membrane is impaired, the absence of AP-3-derived SVs limits the exocytic response3 (Fig. 5b and Extended Data Fig. 14a). In the absence of VAMP7, loss of AP-3 limits release even at a low frequency (Extended Data Fig. 14b), presumably owing to the absence of low-release-probability SVs made by AP-3.
