While recently proposed approaches for aerobe–anaerobe classification show comparable overall accuracy32,61,62, they exhibited lower predictive capacities for obligate anaerobes that encode Cox compared with the OFOR–ODH-based classifier, falsely classifying some as aerobes (accuracies of 0.9 and 0.76; Supplementary Fig. 9 and Supplementary Table 16). For the classifier based on aerobe–anaerobe-associated genes62, the inclusion and predominance of terminal-oxidase-related genes (that is, terminal oxidase subunits and biosynthesis proteins for terminal oxidase haem groups) in the top contributing genes for aerobe prediction may have contributed to the false predictions. Thus, although the presence of Cox is often implemented as an indicator for potential for aerobiosis, cultivation and comparative genomics here indicate that caution must be taken in interpreting the physiology of Cox-containing organisms, including those of Heimdallarchaeia.

Promethearchaeota, including HC1 and other recently reported Cox-encoding Heimdallarchaeia31,32, exhibit OFOR–ODH abundances similar to anaerobic isolates (Fig. 5a–d). Applying the OFOR–ODH-based classifiers, all the analysed genomes of Heimdallarchaeia were consistently predicted to be anaerobic with high confidence regardless of the presence or absence of Cox (mean maximum posterior probabilities of 0.98 ± 0.04 and 0.97 ± 0.06 for LR and LDA; Supplementary Tables 16 and 17). Nearly all other Promethearchaeota genomes were also confidently classified as anaerobic. Classification based on aerobe–anaerobe-associated genes62 also predicted most Cox-encoding Heimdallarchaeia, including HC1, as anaerobic (maximum posterior probabilities of 0.97 ± 0.12 and 0.96 ± 0.09 for LR and LDA, for those predicted as anaerobes). For lineages encoding Cox, this pattern suggests that terminal oxidases are more likely to function in aerotolerance rather than supporting canonical aerobic respiration. We illustrate the ferredoxin-centric metabolisms of HC1 in Fig. 4.

A specific comparison of Promethearchaeota with other archaea yielded a similar pattern. Although archaea capable of aerobic growth often retain ferredoxin-dependent metabolism despite exposure to O2, their OFOR repertoires were genomically distinct from those of obligate anaerobes. Nearly all aerobic isolates (334 out of 340 isolates, or 97%) encoded OFOR containing the POR, POR_N and PFOR_II domains that accounted for more than one-third of their OFORs, whereas, for obligately anaerobic isolates, this OFOR represented no more than one-third of their OFORs (Supplementary Table 18). All analysed Heimdallarchaeia also showed low relative abundances of this aerobe-associated OFOR. Accordingly, their abundances of other OFORs and ODHs were distinct from those of aerobic archaea and instead similar to those of obligately anaerobic archaea and bacteria (Fig. 5d).

Although a recent metagenomic survey proposed aerobic lifestyles for Hodarchaeales based on occurrence of Cox-harbouring MAGs in oxic environments including pelagic habitats (for example, epi-, bathy- and hadal-pelagic)32, all such MAGs were derived from sediments (that is, benthic), where oxygen exposure is highly ambiguous given that concentrations typically decline sharply below the surface63. Moreover, Hodarchaeales were detected in public metagenomic datasets annotated as derived from oxygen-associated environments32, but the presence of oxygen is unclear given that these are sediment samples or oxygen concentrations are either below the detection limit or not measured.

Consistent with this, most Promethearchaeota species—including HC1 and Cox-containing Heimdallarchaeia—have oxygen-sensitive NiFe hydrogenases, reflecting dependence on anaerobic metabolism. Promethearchaeota nearly universally possess group 3c and/or 4g hydrogenases (Supplementary Table 19). In Heimdallarchaeia, the orders Heimdallarchaeales, Gerdarchaeales and Hodarchaeales each generally conserve group 4g (92%), 3b/3c/4g (92%/80%/80%) and 3c (90%) hydrogenases, respectively (Supplementary Table 20). The widespread conservation of ferredoxin-oxidizing hydrogenases (groups 3c and 4g) further supports reliance on a ferredoxin-centred, anaerobic metabolic strategy across Promethearchaeota, including Heimdallarchaeia. Analysis of computed gene expressivity across all archaeal species representatives in GTDB release 220 suggests that anaerobic peptidotrophy is also widely conserved across Promethearchaeota (Fig. 3f, Methods, Supplementary Table 21 and Supplementary Note 12). The coupling of the two would implicate anaerobic H2-evolving peptidotrophy as a widely conserved feature of Promethearchaeota, which agrees with our previous hypothesis4 and phylogenetic analyses tracing organotrophic H2 production and acetogenesis through the Wood–Ljungdahl pathway to the Promethearchaeota ancestor7,64.

Given this broadly anaerobic metabolic framework, we next considered when these archaea may have acquired Cox-mediated aerotolerance. Phylogenetic analyses of the Cox complex based on a concatenated alignment (Cox1–3), Cox1 and Cox3 all show Heimdallarchaeales sequences nested within those of Hodarchaeales (Fig. 5e–g and Supplementary Fig. 10c–e). These topologies do not show evidence for the presence of Cox at the common ancestor of Hodarchaeales and Heimdallarchaeales and suggest that Heimdallarchaeales acquired Cox horizontally from Hodarchaeales.

Here we isolated two strains from the archaeal lineage that descended from the last common ancestor of archaea and eukaryotes—Heimdallarchaeia—and reveal insights into their biology. Anaerobiosis, the absence of persistent intracellular structures and membrane protrusions are conserved among all cultured members, P. syntrophicum MK-D13,4, ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5, ‘Ca. N. marumarumayae’26, strains HC1 and SC1, and a recent Heimdallarchaeaceae enrichment culture40. Dependence on peptides and syntrophy for energy metabolism is also consistent across those with detailed physiological characterization3,5. These organisms further exhibit symbiotic, protrusion-mediated intercellular attachment, linking cell morphology with syntrophic interactions. The conservation of these physiological features across strains spanning two Promethearchaeota classes points towards an anaerobic, peptide-degrading and H2-evolving LAECA that lacked persistent internal structures but possessed membrane-based protrusions.

Consistent with this, members of the phylum, including all cultured strains, lack many pathways for biosynthesis of amino acids, vitamins and nucleotides (Supplementary Table 22), indicating metabolic dependence on partner organisms. Moreover, slow growth is also conserved across all cultured strains and, if LAECA also shared this feature, it may have contributed to key processes in eukaryogenesis (Supplementary Note 13). Although it is unclear whether LAECA possessed Cox, cultivation and comparative genomics indicate that Cox in Heimdallarchaeia are unlikely to function in oxygen respiration. Together, these observations suggest that the prokaryote–eukaryote transition may have involved a physiological shift from an anaerobic to (facultatively) aerobic lifestyle10, alongside major structural innovations. If LAECA was anaerobic but possessed aerotolerance like HC1 (and potentially other Heimdallarchaeia), this feature could have supported interaction with a mitochondrial ancestor under low-oxygen or fluctuating redox conditions, where oxygen reduction by the bacterial partner may have alleviated oxygen toxicity. This relationship is also consistent with the ‘Ox–Tox’ model positing that the mitochondrial progenitor had a role in oxygen detoxification for an anaerobic host65.

Although the extremely small cell size and slow growth rate of P. syntrophicum MK-D1, the only publicly available Promethearchaeota strain3,4, had posed a major obstacle, efforts in cultivation here led to the isolation of two strains that have larger cell sizes, higher growth rates, shorter lag phases and a closer relationship to eukaryotes. These make the strains promising model organisms for exploring the biology of Promethearchaeota that can catalyse investigations of cellular and physiological transitions underlying the emergence of eukaryotic complexity.

The biofilm samples were collected from a gas production well, KTG3, in the Southern Kanto gas field (Chiba Prefecture, Japan). The biofilm was located on a wall of the separator discharge outlet at a depth of 20–40 cm below the water surface. Samples were taken after eruption of brine on 29 August 2019, 16 July 2020 and 11 May 2023 (Extended Data Fig. 1). The gas field is located in an old marine forearc basin and is based on subsurface gas reservoirs in turbidite sandstones, making it geologically and geochemically relevant to past seawater and marine sediment66. The brine from the well KTG3 is rich in organic matter, iodine and iron. Detailed site information has been described previously37 and geochemical characteristics of the brine in the well KTG3 are provided in Extended Data Fig. 1b. The collected biofilm sample was placed in a 100 ml glass bottle filled with brine (no head space) and brought back to our laboratory under refrigerated conditions. The samples were also inoculated in 50 ml glass vials containing anaerobic medium onsite (Supplementary Note 2). Our iTag analysis showed that the biofilm contained abundant and diverse microorganisms, mostly affiliated with uncultured or cultivation-limited microbial groups, including Promethearchaeota. To isolate new Promethearchaeota strains from the samples, we used a strategic batch-type cultivation35 that incorporated previous knowledge and our expectations for this archaeal group (Supplementary Note 1). Detailed information about the cultivation, including the medium composition and purity checks for the HC1 and SC1 cultures, is provided in the Supplementary Methods. Unless otherwise indicated, the HC1 and SC1 cultures were grown in casamino acids–peptone–yeast extract medium (each at 0.005%, w/v) and casamino acids–powdered milk–polypeptone peptone–yeast extract medium (each at 0.005%, 0.005%, 0.01% and 0.05%, w/v), respectively, with an inoculum size of 16% (v/v) for HC1 and 20% (v/v) for SC1. To measure the dissolved oxygen concentrations in KTG3 culture medium lacking reducing agents, we used a fibre optic oxygen meter (Fibox 3 trace, Presence) in combination with an oxygen sensor (SP-PSt6-YAU). The SP-PSt6-YAU sensor was affixed to the inner wall of the 50 ml serum glass bottles using oxygen-permeable silicone adhesive.

DNA extraction, PCR mixture preparation and quantitative PCR (qPCR) analysis were performed as described previously4,67. PCR primers for qPCR used in this study were designed using the probe design tool of ARB program68. The specificity of new primers was confirmed using BLAST and the ARB-SILVA database (https://www.arb-silva.de/)69. The primers and PCR conditions are shown in Supplementary Table 23. The doubling times of cultured archaea were calculated based on the semilogarithmic plot of the qPCR data. For iTag analysis, a universal primer pair 530F/907R, which contained overhang adapters at 5′ ends, was used70. The procedures used for library construction, sequencing and data analysis were described previously4. All samples for data acquisition were checked for growth and microbial composition by qPCR and iTag before or after the experiments.

To evaluate the temperature range for growth, a pure co-culture of HC1 and a tri-culture of SC1 were incubated at a range of 10 °C to 45 °C or 10 °C to 50 °C. All incubations were performed in triplicate. After a certain period of incubation, 16S rRNA gene copy numbers of each strain were evaluated by qPCR.

To examine substrate use of the cultured archaeal strains, the basal media were supplemented with each substrate sterilized either by autoclaving or filtration. We performed two successive transfers under the same cultivation conditions and conducted qPCR targeting the archaeal strains’ 16S rRNA genes in both the first and second subcultures. All incubations were performed in duplicates at the optimum growth temperature for each strain.

To assess the effect of non-proteinaceous substrates on growth of archaeal strains, we added individual substrates to culture medium containing casamino acids–peptone–yeast extract for HC1 and casamino acids–powdered milk–polypeptone peptone–yeast extract for SC1. Each cultivation condition was performed in duplicate.

An epifluorescence microscope (BX53, EVIDENT) equipped with a phase-contrast objective lens and a colour CCD camera system (DP80 or DP75, EVIDENT) was used for routine microscopy observation, with image acquisition and recording performed using cellSense v.4.3 (EVIDENT). When it was necessary to obtain images without cell movement due to Brownian motion, agarose-coated glass slides were used71. Cell and protrusion diameters of HC1 were measured from phase-contrast images using Fiji, an image analysis software based on ImageJ72.

For SEM analysis, archaeal cells were fixed by adding 2.5% (w/v) glutaraldehyde and incubating for 2 h under anoxic conditions at their optimum growth temperatures and then overnight at 4 °C. The sample preparation procedure was performed as described previously3. The samples were observed under an extreme-high-resolution focused ion beam (FIB)-SEM (Helios G4 UX, Thermo Fisher Scientific) system operated at 1 kV.

To evaluate the volumes and numbers of HC1 cell bodies, protrusions and membrane vesicles under different yeast extract concentrations, we acquired wide-area SEM images using Maps v.2.5 (Thermo Fisher Scientific), which was installed in the FIB-SEM operation system. Wide-area images were obtained by stitching 100 images into a larger 10 × 10 image, with each image taken with an acceleration voltage of 1 kV, a beam current of 13 pA, a field of view of 36.3 µm × 24.2 µm and an image resolution of 23.6 nm per pixel. The acquired wide-area SEM images were then analysed using AMIRA 3D Pro 2024.1 and 2024.2 software (Thermo Fisher Scientific). First, the images were denoised by applying curvature-driven diffusion73. Next, HC1 cell bodies, protrusions, membrane vesicles and Methanocalculus cells were segmented with the aid of a deep-learning module based on PyTorch74 and Keras (https://github.com/fchollet/keras). The deep learning model created from 2,000 × 2,000 pixels was adapted to the full images, followed by manual modification and watershed segmentation. Each segmented component, except for protrusions, was labelled and the area and perimeter were analysed. Protrusions were skeletonized using the Auto Skeleton module75, and the number of fibre segments and their curved length were measured after excluding looped fibres or those shorter than 10 pixels.

For the preparation of ultrathin sections of archaeal cells for TEM, we followed a previously established protocol3. The section samples were observed using a conventional TEM (Tecnai 20, FEI) system at an acceleration voltage of 120 kV. Detailed information about observations of HC1’s membrane vesicles and thin filaments on the surface of SC1 protrusions is described in the Supplementary Methods.

For QFDE-EM observations, archaeal cultures (440 ml of HC1 culture and 25 ml of SC1 culture) were concentrated to approximately 5 ml through filtration using a 0.22-µm-pore-size polyethersulfone (PES) filter unit (Corning) and transferred to a glass vial in an anaerobic chamber (95:5 (v/v) N2:H2 atmosphere; COY Laboratory Products). To remove the H2, which is inhibitory to the strains, this vial’s headspace was replaced with N2/CO2 gas (80:20, v/v) through flushing. The subsequent procedure was performed as described previously3,76.

Before EM observation, 2 ml of culture liquid was taken from a culture bottle using a syringe, and the culture liquid was concentrated to approximately 50 µl by centrifugation at 20,400g for 10 min at 20 °C. Then, 3 µl of the concentrated liquid culture was applied onto a glow-discharged Quantifoil Mo grid R2/1 (Quantifoil MicroTools) after mixing with 15 nm gold colloids (Electron Microscopy Sciences) and plunge-frozen into liquid ethane using the Vitrobot Mark IV (Thermo Fisher Scientific) at 4 °C and 95% humidity. The frozen grids were screened on a 626 side-entry cryoholder (Gatan) with a 200 kV JEM2200FS electron microscope (JEOL). Suitable grids were processed for cryo-ET in the 300 kV Titan Krios G4 electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) equipped with a bottom-mounted Selectris X energy filter (slit width, 5 eV) and a Falcon 4i direct detector camera. Tile series of each specimen were collected at a nominal magnification of ×19,500, resulting in an image resolution of 6.19 Å per pixel, and a dose symmetric tile scheme was performed between +60° and −60° at 2° increments using Tomography software implemented on a TITAN Krios G4, resulting in a total electron dose of 91.5 electrons per Å2. The tilt series was aligned with gold fiducials, and tomograms were reconstructed using filtered back projection or SIRT in the IMOD software77 with an image binning of 5. Segmentations of HC1’s cellular components were performed using AMIRA 3D Pro software. Cellular membranes and granular structures were segmented manually with the help of a deep-learning module, and actin filaments were segmented manually.

Cryo-EM images and tomograms shown in Extended Data Fig. 2i–n and Supplementary Video 2 were acquired using the CRYO ARM 300 II (JEOL) system. Detailed procedures for sample preparation and imaging conditions are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

The protocol for antibody preparation and observation by immunofluorescence for lokiactin generally followed that of a previous study5. The lokiactin antibodies were made using peptides specific for the lokiactin sequences of HC1 and SC1 (Supplementary Fig. 3). The regions of the peptides are the same region as the peptides for ‘Ca. L. ossiferum’5. We made three antibodies in total (that is, ab1 for HC1; ab1 for SC1; and ab2 for both strains), and all of them were created using the service of Cosmo Bio and validated by enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay. Detailed procedures of western blotting and immunofluorescence staining are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

Cells were fixed under anoxic conditions by adding paraformaldehyde solution (methanol-free, formaldehyde solution, 16% (w/v), Electron Microscopy Sciences) to a final concentration of 4% (v/v) directly into the culture bottles and incubating for 2–3 h at 4 °C. After fixation, cells were washed with PBS (153.8 mM NaCl, 2.7 mM Na2HPO4, 1.5 mM KH2PO4 (pH 7.2)). Subsequently, cells were stored in 50% ethanol with PBS at −30 °C until use in subsequent experiments. The design of specific probes and hybridization chain reaction (HCR)-FISH were performed in accordance with previously described protocols4,78. A list of the 16S rRNA-targeted oligonucleotide probes used in this study is provided in Supplementary Table 24. Cells were counterstained with DAPI in the ProLong Diamond Antifade Mountant with DAPI (Thermo Fisher Scientific). FISH images were acquired using a STELLARIS STED confocal microscope (Leica) with a ×100/1.4 NA oil-immersion or ×93/1.3 NA glycerol-immersion objective lens at ×2 or ×6 zoom, a line-scanning frequency of 400 or 700 Hz and a line average of 3. Fluorescence signals were detected in confocal mode at 405, 499 and 553 nm for excitation, and some images were deconvolved using the adaptive Lightning strategy in LasX software (Leica) when necessary. The 3D video was constructed from 27 sections of 8.17 μm thick using the LasX software. Line-intensity profiles were obtained using LasX software for each of the DAPI and Alexa Fluor 488 channels along a line through the centre of the target cell.

To measure peptides and proteins, culture liquid samples were filtered through a 0.2 µm pore-size polytetrafluoroethylene filter unit (Merck Millipore) before sample preservation and analysis. The molecular mass distribution of peptides and proteins was determined using an UPLC system equipped with the ACQUITY UPLC Protein BEH SEV column (Waters) as described previously79.

Methane concentrations in the headspace of culture bottles were measured by gas chromatography as described previously4.

Measurement of haem B was performed according to the previously reported method80. For this measurement, archaeal cultures (440 ml of HC1, and 900 ml of P. syntrophicum MK-D1) were first concentrated to about 5 ml using a 0.22-µm-pore-size PES filter unit (Corning) on a clean bench. The concentrated cell suspensions were then further concentrated by pelleting the cells through centrifugation at 20,400g for 10 min at 4 °C. The collected cells were washed twice with their respective basal medium without energy substrates.

Nitrate and nitrite concentrations were measured by high-performance liquid chromatography (LC) using the TSKgel SAX column (Tosoh, 35 mm × 4.6 mm inner diameter) with 3% (w/v) NaCl as the eluent. The column temperature was maintained at 40 °C, and detection was performed using a UV-VIS detector (GL-7451, GL Science) as described previously81.

Iron concentrations in the brine were determined by quadrupole inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (ICP-MS; iCAP Qc, Thermo Fisher Scientific). To prevent metal precipitation before measuring the total iron concentrations, brine samples were acidified with high-purity concentrated HNO3 (TAMAPURE AA-100, Tama Chemical) at a final concentration of 1.5 M. For ICP-MS analysis, the water sample was diluted with 0.3 M HNO3, and four internal standards (Be, Sc, Y and In) were added to correct instrument drift. Mass interferences were eliminated using the kinetic energy discrimination mode with H2 reaction gas for high-sensitivity 56Fe analysis.

Genomic DNA from HC1 and SC1 was extracted according to a previous protocol67. Whole-genome sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced using the Illumina MiSeq system, with additional mate-pair sequencing for HC1 and Oxford Nanopore PromethION sequencing for SC1. Detailed procedures of genome assembly, gene prediction and functional annotation are described in the Supplementary Methods.

For RNA-based sequencing analysis, total RNA was extracted from HC1 and SC1 cells collected during their exponential growth phase. Specifically, cells were collected from a 25 ml HC1 culture grown for 25 days and a 50 ml SC1 culture grown for 51 days. To concentrate the cells, the cultures were first filtered through a 0.22-µm-pore-size PES filter unit (Corning) on a clean bench, reducing the volume to approximately 4 ml, and then centrifuged at 20,400g for 10 min at 4 °C for further concentration. Derailed procedures of RNA extraction, RNA-seq library preparation, sequencing and quantification of gene expression are provided in the Supplementary Methods.

For proteomic analysis, HC1, SC1 and P. syntrophicum MK-D1 were cultured under the conditions described in the Supplementary Methods. After confirming growth by qPCR, cells were concentrated using a PES filter unit followed by centrifugation, as done for the samples used in western blotting analysis. The collected cell samples were washed once with the basal medium lacking energy substrates, then suspended in 200 µl of 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate (pH 8.6) containing 2 mM phenylmethylsulfonyl fluoride. Cells were disrupted by sonication at 2 °C using a Q700 sonicator (QSonica) operating at 40 kHz. The protein concentration of the cell-free extract was determined by a Qubit fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). All subsequent procedures, including LC–tandem MS (LC–MS/MS) data acquisitions and data analysis, were performed as described previously82,83.

Glycoproteome analysis was performed using the same culture samples as those used for proteome analysis. The procedure was identical up to the point of cell disruption by sonication, after which half of the protein extract samples were allocated for glycoproteome analysis. Subsequent sample preparation, LC–MS/MS analysis and data processing were performed as previously described46,84.

ESPs in Promethearchaeota genomes were annotated using HMMER v.3.4 (hmmsearch)85 and HMM profiles are available from InterPro86. Hits were determined based on an e-value cut-off of 0.0001 and a bit score above the gathering threshold (GA) specified in each HMM profile. Distant hits were identified based on less stringent thresholds for e value (0.01) and bit score (GA-10). We annotated homologues of elongation factor 2 and DNA polymerase epsilon based on (1) distant homology with PFAM domains found in eukaryotic elongation factor 2 (PF00679, PF14492 and/or PF03764) and DNA polymerase epsilon (PF00136 and PF03104); (2) alignment using MAFFT (v.7.525; default options)87 with representatives of bacterial, archaeal and eukaryotic homologues annotated with the above domains in UniProtKB (release 2026_01)88 and clustered with 60% sequence identity (MMseqs2 v.17.b804f)89; (3) trimming with trimAl (v.1.5.0; -gt 0.1)90; (4) tree construction with FastTree (v.2.1.11; -lg)91; and (5) identification of Promethearchaeota homologues that form a sister group with eukaryotic sequences

Promethearchaeota genomes were collected from the Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) release 22092 and GenBank. Genomes not included in GTDB r220 were classified into species-level lineages defined in GTDB or new species based on sequence distances estimated using MASH (v.2.3)93. Coding sequences were predicted using Prokka (v.1.14.6)94 with the default parameters and annotated with eggnog-mapper (v.2.1.12)95 and the eggnog (v.5.0) database using the default parameters96. For constructing a genome-based phylogeny of Promethearchaeota, the following single-copy marker genes defined by GTDB were used for phylogenetic tree construction (Supplementary Table 25). Maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny was performed using IQTREE v.2.3.5 with ultrafast bootstrapping97, a concatenated alignment of these marker genes trimmed using BMGE v.1.12 (-m BLOSUM30 -g 0.67 -b 3)98 and a universal distribution model (UDM0064 LCLR) as previously described99. Maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny for the 16S rRNA gene was performed using a sequence alignment generated with MAFFT (--maxiterate 1000 --localpair)87, the optimum model selected by ModelFinder (SYM + R6)100 and regular bootstrapping. Bootstrap values were recalculated using BOOSTER (v.0.1.2)101.

For maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny of target genes, we first collected relevant sequences by using amino acid sequences obtained from Promethearchaeota as the query and searching against genes belonging to the same protein family collected from GTDB r220 species representatives92. For this, the MMseqs2 v.16.747c6 search command102 was used with three iterative searches with different sensitivities from sensitivity level 4 to 8.5 (--min-seq-id 0.3 -c 0.7). To select representative sequences for tree construction, we (1) clustered the collected sequences using the MMseqs2 cluster command102 (--min-seq-id 0.6 -c 0.7); (2) constructed a rough tree using FastTreeMP (v.2.1.11)91 with an alignment generated with MAFFT (v.7.525)87 and trimmed with trimAl v.1.5.0 (-gt 0.1)90; and (3) subsampled phylogenetically representative sequences from the tree using Parnas (v.0.1.6)103. An alignment for the representatives was generated using MAFFT-DASH (--localpair --maxiterate 100 --dash)104 and trimmed using trimAl (-gt 0.3). Finally, we used this as an input for maximum-likelihood estimation of the phylogeny using IQTREE v.3.1.1 with either 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates or 100 bootstrap replicates97, and used ModelFinder100 to identify the best-fitting model among C10, C20, C30, C40, C50 and C60 (LG + CXX + G + F). For bootstrap replicates, transfer bootstrap expectation values were also calculated using BOOSTER (v.0.1.2)101.

For estimation of the phylogeny of the Cox complex, we used a concatenated alignment of subunits 1, 2 and 3. For all archaeal and bacterial species representatives in GTDB release 220, each subunit was identified with hmmsearch85 against the corresponding protein families (PF00115, PF00116 and PF00510) using a domain e-value cut-off of 0.001 and coverage of 50%. Subunits were concatenated if the target organism encoded (1) one copy of each subunit across its genome; or (2) multiple copies but organized one copy of each within 10 loci of each other. For organisms outside of Promethearchaeota, Cox1 was clustered with 50% sequence identity and 80% coverage using MMseqs2 easy-cluster to choose representative sets of Cox1, 2 and 3. Alignment for each subunit and tree construction of the concatenated alignment was performed as described above but with ultrafast bootstrap support (-bb 1000).

Gene expressivity was calculated using cordon56 using ribosomal proteins as a reference and the default settings. Peptidotrophy was annotated based on the presence of extracellular peptidases, glutamate dehydrogenases and glycine dehydrogenases with high expressivity (within the top 25% of each genome), all consistently found in isolates specialized in peptide degradation (strains MK-D1, HC1, SC1, Coprothermobacter proteolyticus, Necrotrophus endoclepta, Porphyromonas gingivalis and Salinivirga cyanobacteriivorans). Anaerobic peptidotrophy was annotated if high-expressivity OFORs and FeFe or NiFe hydrogenases were also present. Those with NiFe hydrogenase-containing gene sets homologous to those highly expressed by syntrophic Promethearchaeota isolates or archaeal electron-bifurcating hydrogenase MvhADG–HdrABC were further annotated as H2-evolving. Aerobic peptidotrophy was annotated based on the presence of a high-expressivity Cox (within top 50% of each genome) along with a complete complex III (cytochrome b/b6 with a cytochrome c, Rieske FeS protein and/or a copper-binding electron carrier like plastocyanin or halocyanin). Aerotolerant peptidotrophy was annotated based on the presence of a high-expressivity Cbd with type 1 or 2 NADH:quinone oxidoreductase but lacking the ability to transfer all electrons from peptide degradation to oxygen reduction. Different expressivity thresholds were used for peptide metabolism and terminal oxidases based on the observation that expressivity tends to be in the 25–50% range for archaea that are known to be aerobic (that is, Halobacteriales).

For prediction of aerobic capacity in Promethearchaeota genomes, classifiers were trained using a dataset of strains with annotated aerobic capacity derived from BacDive105. Strains were categorized as obligate aerobes, diazotrophic aerobes, facultative (an)aerobes and obligate anaerobes (with and without Cox). For classification, obligate aerobes, diazotrophic aerobes and facultative (an)aerobes were grouped as organisms with aerobic capacity, whereas obligate anaerobes were grouped as lacking aerobic capacity. Host-associated and phototrophic organisms (including oxygenic and anoxygenic phototrophs such as purple and green bacteria) were excluded, as host-associated oxygen gradients and light-driven metabolism can decouple oxygen exposure from intrinsic respiratory strategies, thereby confounding the relationship between genomic features and metabolic lifestyle. BacDive annotations were manually curated based on literature information and genomic annotation.

For genomic annotation, strains annotated as obligate aerobes in BacDive but encoding pathways for anaerobic respiration (that is, dissimilatory nitrate reduction or sulfate reduction) were reclassified as facultative anaerobes. Dissimilatory nitrate reduction and sulfate reduction were annotated based on the presence of genes with the following PFAM domains: Molybdopterin, Molydop_binding, Nitr_red_alph_N or NapB for dissimilatory nitrate reductases, and APS_reductase_C for adenylyl-sulfate reductase. Diazotrophy was annotated for isolates harbouring genes containing the PFAM domain Oxidored_nitro.

Strains classified as obligate anaerobes without experimental evidence of growth under aerobic conditions were excluded. Likewise, strains classified as facultative anaerobes without experimental evidence of enhanced growth under aerobic conditions were removed as they may rather be oxygen-tolerant anaerobes.

For each genome, OFOR and ODH abundance was calculated as log((n + 1)/genome size (Mb)), where n corresponds to the number of OFOR or ODH homologues. Genes encoding OFOR and ODH were annotated based on PFAM annotations generated by eggNOG-mapper (v.2.1.2)95. OFORs were identified based on the presence of PFAM domain combinations ‘POR,POR_N’, ‘PFOR_II,POR_N’, ‘POR_N,TPP_enzyme_C’ or ‘PFOR_II,TPP_enzyme_C’. OFORs containing three domains were annotated using hmmsearch and a domain e-value cutoff of 0.00001 and domain coverage cut-off of 0.8. ODH abundance was estimated based on the number of annotated E1 (decarboxylase) subunits (PFAM E1_dh), which determines the substrate specificity and serves as a proxy for the presence of 2-oxoacid dehydrogenase complexes. Genomic frequencies were calculated for the five most discriminative amino acids reported previously61, as these capture the majority of the discriminatory signal while reducing redundancy among correlated amino acid frequencies.

Classification of aerobic capacity based on OFOR and ODH abundance or amino acid frequency was performed using LR and LDA implemented in scikit-learn (v.1.8.0). Features were standardized using z-score normalization before model training. LR was performed with balanced class weights to account for class imbalance. Models were evaluated using stratified k-fold cross-validation (StratifiedKFold; k = 5), in which the dataset was partitioned into training and test sets while preserving the proportion of organisms with and without aerobic capacity in each split. Predictions were generated using cross_val_predict, ensuring that each sample was evaluated in a held-out fold. Classification performance was assessed using accuracy and balanced accuracy based on these out-of-fold predictions. For each genome, posterior probabilities were obtained from the fitted models, and the maximum posterior probability was used as a measure of classification confidence. For Promethearchaeota, only genomes with ≥85% completeness and ≤5% contamination were analysed, with two Hodarchaeales MAGs encoding Cox and Complex I (JBSWRZ01) or Cox, Complex I and Complex III (JBSWRG01) as exceptions.

To quantify the similarity between metabolic categories, the centroid of each category was calculated as the mean of the normalized OFOR abundance and normalized ODH abundance across all genomes in that category. Pairwise distances between category centroids were first computed using Euclidean distance in the two-dimensional feature space: dij = ((xi − xj)2 + (yi − yj)2)0.5, where x and y represent the mean values of normalized OFOR abundance and normalized ODH abundance for categories i and j. These distances quantify the separation between metabolic regimes in the feature space and were visualized as a centroid distance matrix.

Moreover, Mahalanobis distances were calculated to account for the covariance structure of the data. For each pair of category centroids i and j, the Mahalanobis distance was computed as: Dij = (mui – muj)T × Σ–1 × (mui – muj), where mui and muj are the centroid vectors of the two categories and Σ is the pooled covariance matrix estimated from all genomes in the feature space.

To examine archaea specifically, ODH and OFOR abundances were also comparatively analysed for archaeal isolates. Although archaea capable of aerobic growth often use ferredoxin as an electron carrier, such organisms nearly universally conserve a unique OFOR annotatable with three PFAM domains (PFOR_II, POR_N and POR; domain e-value ≤ 0.0001 and domain coverage ≥ 80% based on hmmsearch) (334 out of 340 analysed isolates; Supplementary Table 18). The abundances of ODH and other OFORs were calculated for each archaeal isolate as described above. Promethearchaeota were compared with mesophilic archaea as, for thermophiles, increased temperature decreases oxygen solubility and may therefore influence the interaction between metabolism and oxygen.

Further information on research design is available in the Nature Portfolio Reporting Summary linked to this article.

Genomes for ‘Ca. M. peptidiphilum’ HC1, ‘Ca. F. multiprotrusionum’ SC1 and Methanocalculus sp. strains MC2 and MC3 are available at DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank database under accession numbers AP029002, AP029247, AP029003 and Biosample accession number SAMD00736001, respectively. The iTag sequence data were deposited under BioProject accessions PRJDB19594, PRJDB19596 and PRJDB19597 with SRA accession numbers DRR620266–DRR620297, DRR1044922 and DRR1044923. The 16S rRNA gene sequences of Hodarchaeales HC2 and Heimdallarchaeaceae HC4 obtained from enrichment cultures were deposited in the DDBJ/EMBL/GenBank database under accession numbers LC859055 and LC859056, respectively. The RNA-seq data of HC1 and SC1 were deposited under BioProject PRJDB19599 with SRA accession number DRR620298 and BioProject PRJDB19601 with SRA accession number DRR620299, respectively. The cryo-ETs have been deposited in the EMDB under accession codes EMD-63316, EMD-63317 and EMD-64894 (HC1) and EMD-63318–EMD-63320 and EMD-63267 (SC1). The structural model and density map of HC1 actin filament obtained by sub-tomogram averaging has been deposited under PDB accession 9WC4 and EMDB accession EMD-65855. The proteome and glycoproteome data, including all LC–MS/MS raw files (.raw) and complete protein identification lists (.xlsx), have been deposited in the ProteomeXchange Consortium via jPOSTrepo106 under dataset identifiers PXD059994 (JPST003561) for HC1, PXD059995 (JPST003567) for SC1 and PXD051006 (JPST003012) for P. syntophicum MK-D1.

#1323. Leeds United Must Make Final Daniel Farke Sack Decision After Alarming Slump

Daniel Farke has split the Leeds United fanbase.

Some want to keep the German and feel he deserves a new contract, while others believe he should be sacked and replaced due to the club's disappointing recent run of form. Indeed, the Whites have won just one of their last nine matches across all competitions.

They started the season with back-to-back victories over Nottingham Forest - one in the Premier League and Carabao Cup. Successive draws against Brentford and Brighton & Hove Albion followed, before they earned a thumping 4-1 win against Newcastle United, leaving the Whites inside the Champions League places with eight points from a possible 12.

But Leeds have since failed to kick on and are now without a win in their last five Premier League matches after they were beaten 2-0 at Bournemouth on Saturday. Goals either side of the break from Evanilson and Amine Adli condemned the Whites to a disappointing defeat.

Although Leeds still sit 11th and in a comfortable position in mid-table, fans are concerned about the recent drop off in form, with some questioning Farke's position at Elland Road.

It emerged back in September that Leeds were preparing to offer Farke a new contract, with his current deal set to expire next summer. They felt it would be just reward for the club's impressive start and how they ended last season, finishing up in 14th with 47 points.

Despite Leeds' recent slump, there is no suggestion that Leeds plan on abandoning their decision to extend Farke's contract and think he is the man to lead them forward in the long-term.

And, taking it all into consideration, including the form post-Newcastle, Farke does deserve time to turn Leeds' fortunes around and should not be sacked, at least until Christmas.

He has enough credit in the bank and has shown he can flick the switch, having changed his system last December to ensure the Whites remained as a Premier League club.

There is no reason Farke cannot do that again, but he must allow his attacking players to have more freedom and use a more front-footed approach first. While that could disrupt his side's excellent defensive record, having conceded just eight times in nine top-flight matches this season, they need to find a way to score more goals.

Indeed, Leeds have found the net just nine times in the league and four of those came in the same game against Newcastle. They have a huge reliance on star striker Dominic Calvert-Lewin, who has scored four goals this campaign, and more need to step up and chip in.

A damning statistic that emerged following the defeat at Bournemouth is that out of the 96 teams in Europe's big-five leagues, Leeds rank 95th for final third passing accuracy (56.9%) this season. When taking into account just the Premier League, they rank rock bottom in 20th.

The likes of Harry Wilson, Dan James, Brenden Aaronson and Anton Stach have to do better and are letting Farke down at the moment. They are not producing to the level that is required, and the German may have to change something if performances don't improve, and fast.

Jean-Matteo Bahoya is waiting for his chance to impress, and although Farke issued a 10-minute explanation defending the Frenchman's lack of game time, he should be used more. Leeds are desperate for some attacking impetus, and, as the regular first-team wingers are not impressing, Farke could do no wrong but give Bahoya more minutes.

Saturday's home game against Tottenham does feel crucial for Farke, and if Leeds fail to win, the pressure is no doubt going to rise and the club may pull the trigger. For now though, Farke should be kept at Leeds and given a crack to win the unhappy fans over.

The Whites could be in the market for a new striker in January

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#1322. 'Divisive' teacher's pet who players roll their eyes at? Or obsessive who truly cares? Man United insiders reveal what Bruno Fernandes' team-mates really think of him - as we reveal Michael Carrick decided to drop captain BEFORE his Como rant

Published: 22:00 EDT, 30 October 2026 | Updated: 22:00 EDT, 30 October 2026

The expression on the faces of Manchester United’s players turned to shock and shame as they left the pitch at Old Trafford on Sunday and ran the gauntlet of fan anger.

No sooner had head coach Michael Carrick been cheered down the tunnel after a 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth left him on the brink of the sack than supporters rounded on the team and a torrent of abuse rained down from the Stretford End.

‘It was a wake-up for all the players,’ one source told Daily Mail Sport this week.

For captain Bruno Fernandes, it was a particularly painful moment. Fernandes was still in his tracksuit bottoms and hoodie having been dropped to the bench and left there to stew by Carrick as United’s season hit a new low.

He is used to the adoration of fans, but their reaction was muted to say the least when he left the dugout to warm up in the second half.

It was the culmination of the hardest two weeks of Fernandes’ seven-year career at United.

Bruno Fernandes has had the hardest two weeks of his Man United career. The lowest point came when he was hooked off in a 4-1 defeat in Como - then took aim at Michael Carrick in his post-match interview

Fernandes was left on the bench for United's loss to Bournemouth, and didn't receive the adulation he's used to getting from the home supporters at Old Trafford

The 32-year-old was struggling for form and fitness this season long before Carrick replaced him in the 67th minute of the humiliating 4-1 Champions League defeat by Como.

Afterwards, he was accused of throwing his head coach under the bus by publicly blaming the tactics and lack of bravery for United’s worst European defeat in 32 years.

Fernandes was unaware at the time that his family home in Cheshire had been raided by a gang of three burglars during the game, and only found out as United set off for Manchester. Thankfully, his wife Ana and their two children were away on holiday.

It’s understood Carrick had already made the bold decision to drop Fernandes for the first time in five years, and make Harry Maguire captain against Bournemouth, even before hearing about his comments.

Despite liking an Instagram post saying ‘never push a loyal person to the point where they no longer care’ after the Bournemouth defeat, Fernandes is said to have taken Carrick’s decision on the chin when the team was named on Saturday, just as he has accepted playing in a wider position over recent weeks while Youri Tielemans has stepped into the No 10 role.

Although Carrick and Fernandes were both at Carrington on Monday as speculation raged over the head coach’s future, the player had left before Carrick turned up just before 2pm. The Portuguese was having treatment on a niggling injury that has troubled him since the World Cup.

Once United had clarified Carrick’s position, the two men met at the training ground and cleared the air on Tuesday.

Carrick has since confirmed Fernandes will remain as captain and is set to lead the side against Chelsea at Stamford Bridge this lunchtime in what is a huge game for United and their manager.

Others have been less forgiving. Jamie Carragher branded Fernandes’ comments in Como ‘disgraceful’, while Alan Shearer believes he has tarnished his legacy at Old Trafford.

Carrick and Fernandes have cleared the air at Carrington and Fernandes will remain as United's captain, starting at Chelsea today

But the Portuguese's actions have reignited the debate over whether Fernandes is too emotional to wear the armband

The controversy has reignited the debate over whether Fernandes is too emotional to wear the armband. Former United boss Ole Gunnar Solskjaer said so in a video clip that resurfaced last week, explaining why he preferred Maguire.

That was put to Carrick, who was part of Solskjaer’s coaching team at the time, and he said: ‘There are different personalities, characteristics and ways to lead.

‘The questions get asked, and I understand why you're asking them now. He cares deeply about this football club and about the team and he's desperate to do well.’

It is a view backed up by some sources who describe a football obsessive who takes United’s problems to heart and feels the pain of the alarming slump this season just as keenly as the fans. While other players have distractions away from the pitch (too many in Gary Neville’s opinion), they say Fernandes can find no escape.

He is understood to have been worn down by yet another United crisis just when it seemed the good times were coming back under Carrick. Inevitably, that has taken its toll and has not been helped by worries over his future at Old Trafford as talks over a new contract drag on.

Insiders describe him as ‘an emotional metronome’ who sets the mood around the club, both good and bad. They say he bonds the dressing room together, and question who else in the United squad should wear the armband.

However, some of Fernandes’ team-mates in recent years have seen him as a more divisive figure whose close relationship with Ruben Amorim was viewed with suspicion.

‘The players can be quite dismissive of him,’ said a source close to one. ‘Sometimes they roll their eyes when he’s talking.’

Not surprisingly, Fernandes’ form has suffered this season with his four goals and one assist coming in United’s only two wins against Ipswich Town and Sabah – months after he picked up the Premier League Player of the Year award for his nine goals and Premier League record 21 assists last term.

He brought his trophy into Carrington and posed for individual pictures with staff from the treatment room to the canteen to thank them for the part they played in his success.

‘The players can be quite dismissive of him,’ said a source close to one of Fernandes' team-mates. ‘Sometimes they roll their eyes when he’s talking’

Insiders describe him as ‘an emotional metronome’ who sets the mood around the club, both good and bad

‘He has been the club's best player over the past few seasons and we need to get the best out of him for this team to succeed,’ legendary United captain Bryan Robson told Daily Mail Sport.

‘I have always thought a captain should be a centre back or deep-lying midfielder so they can see the game and spot things when they go wrong.

‘The trouble for Bruno is he is playing in a more advanced position because we have no centre forward. He's constantly looking over his shoulder and not necessarily expending his energy in the right way.

‘He gets how important it is to keep the group together. I know he has been instrumental as captain in organising bonding dinners and days out. That helps, but he also must know the importance of keeping things in the dressing room.’

With the Como controversy behind him, Fernandes is said to have returned to being the best version of himself during what has been a turbulent week for everyone at United.

Stung by the reaction from fans on Sunday, he has taken what is described as ‘direct action’ to lift the rest of the players and confront the crisis, as a captain should. Now another test of his leadership awaits at Stamford Bridge.

Good evening and welcome to our live coverage of this Europa League tie between Bournemouth and AC Milan at the Vitality Stadium.

Back in 2008, Bournemouth’s prospect of a European meeting with Milan seemed impossible. After entering administration with crippling debts of around £4m, Bournemouth were handed a 10-point deduction and relegated from League One. To make matters worse, a hefty 17-point deduction was given to the club ahead of the 2008-09 League Two season, with relegation to non-league seeming inevitable. However, midway through the campaign, the transformative Eddie Howe was parachuted in as Bournemouth’s saviour, eventually guiding the club to safety.

Fast forward to October 2026 in an extraordinary rise and Bournemouth are competing in their first-ever European campaign in the club’s 127-year existence. They welcome Milan to Dorset, having earned back-to-back victories over Real Sociedad and Sturm Graz to kick off their inaugural Europa League adventure in style.

Now, they host the second most successful side in the European Cup history. In terms of heritage and silverware, these clubs could not be further apart, but on the pitch, it’s incredibly tough to call.

On Sunday, Marco Rose’s Bournemouth picked up their first Premier League win of the season, beating 10-man Sunderland 2-0 at the Vitality thanks to goals from Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson to move out of the relegation zone.

Meanwhile, Ruben Amorim is in charge at Milan and returns to England after a tumultuous 14-month reign at Manchester United, where he was sacked in January. Milan lost their opening Europa League fixture 2-0 at home to Benfica, before battering Salzburg 4-0 in Austria, with Alphadjo Cisse netting a stunning hat-trick.

Crystal Palace are also in the Europa League tonight and face an incredibly daunting away trip to Turkish side Besiktas. Pressure is firmly on manager Pierre Sage following the 5-0 humiliation against Brighton last weekend and a shaky start to the season. Palace lost 3-2 to Sage’s former employers Lyon in their previous Europa League outing, with a positive performance and result needed to restore the fans’ faith.

Both games kick-off at 20:00, with team news coming imminently.

#1320. Van Bronckhorst warns Feyenoord: ‘Win over Como guarantees nothing against Inter’

Giovanni van Bronckhorst has warned that Feyenoord’s home win over Como counts for little ahead of Tuesday’s Champions League clash with Inter in Rotterdam.

With quotes via TuttoMercatoWeb, citing FCInter1908, the Feyenoord coach spoke at his pre-match press conference before the game at De Kuip. It kicks off at 21:00 CET [20:00 GMT] and will be refereed by Sweden’s Glenn Nyberg.

“Getting a result against an Italian team doesn’t mathematically mean we’ll win again,” Van Bronckhorst said. “Of course, we watched the Como game too, but tomorrow the opponent will be different. Como are in the Champions League for the first time, Inter have a different status. Every team has its vulnerabilities, though.”

Inter arrive in the Netherlands after their first league defeat of the season, a 3-1 loss to Milan in Saturday’s derby, which leaves them three points behind leaders Lazio. Cristian Chivu is also short of players, with Lautaro Martínez, Benjamin Pavard, John Stones, Curtis Jones and Luis Henrique all out injured.

Van Bronckhorst played as a left-back for Barcelona and Arsenal. He confirmed that Shaqueel van Persie and Reiss Nelson have trained and will be available.

“I’ve watched several Inter games, including the last one against Milan,” Van Bronckhorst said. “Playing against them is difficult, they play football similar to ours. They have a lot of injuries, but also a lot of quality and experience.

“Inter aren’t afraid to sit in a low block and then press high, they bring a lot of players forward, and they’re a complete team. They’re missing some players, and we’ll have our chances to win the game, as has always been the case.

“Tomorrow’s Inter will be different from the one we saw against Barcelona, but they know what to do in the Champions League to go through and be successful. Tomorrow we need to play our cards well and try to get a great result. We’ve struggled away from home, while we’ve already won at home against Como. Let’s hope we can do it again.”

Feyenoord are without a win in three games, and van Bronckhorst wants his side to repeat what worked against Como. “The group has energy. It knows it’s come from three games without a win and wants to show tomorrow that it wants to turn the page,” he said. “We don’t need to run more, but to be compact at certain moments of the game. We managed that against Como, and we need to do it again so we don’t leave Inter dangerous spaces.”

He also played down the derby result. “I didn’t look at the result, but at the way they played. They’re a top team, and not just this year. They have players who know what to do in the Champions League. I have to focus on their strengths, not on the result of their last game.”

#1318. Aston Villa threatening Jamie Carragher with legal action over 'insults' looks wild... but this is why club's billionaire owner Nassef Sawiris has had enough, writes TOM COLLOMOSSE

Published: 07:00 EDT, 31 October 2026 | Updated: 08:54 EDT, 31 October 2026

Before billionaires Nassef Sawiris and Wes Edens took control of Aston Villa in summer 2018, the club were staring into the abyss.

Villa had just lost the Championship play-off final to Fulham and facing another year without Premier League funds, the club’s financial future was uncertain.

Eight years later, Villa have qualified for the Champions League for the second year in three. In Unai Emery, they have one of the world’s best coaches.

Despite significant issues navigating Premier League and UEFA financial rules, they lifted the Europa League last season and look well-equipped to challenge for a top-five finish again this term. In Sawiris’ time, they have made two £100million sales – Jack Grealish to Manchester City for £100m in 2021, and Morgan Rogers to Chelsea for £117m last summer, while investing hugely in players and making Emery one of the world’s best-paid coaches. Villa are also taking the capacity of Villa Park past 50,000.

By any measure, this is a club on the rise and Sawiris should feel very proud of what they have achieved during his tenure.

So you can imagine his irritation when Emery, the club’s most valuable asset, is being pushed towards the Manchester United job by a high-profile pundit like Jamie Carragher, apparently because Villa is not big enough for him. That said, the post that landed on Villa’s X account at 10.16pm on Friday still took the breath away.

Aston Villa is a club on the rise and Sawiris (above) should feel very proud of what they have achieved during his tenure

Jamie Carragher has been pushing Unai Emery towards the Manchester United job on The Overlap podcast, claiming that Villa 'will never be' United (source: TheOverlap/YouTube)

‘Aston Villa will initiate legal action against Jamie Carragher for his unacceptable insults about the Club and its fans.

‘Aston Villa will not allow anyone to stop our ascension in English and European football. Nassef Sawiris, Chairman.’

It is unclear which ‘insults’ drove Sawiris to this step. Carragher has talked up Emery’s candidacy for United on different platforms and received the inevitable backlash from Villa supporters online. Carragher doubled down on his view on The Overlap podcast this week, in which he told ‘Aston Villa fans’ to ‘shut the f*** up.’

He continued: ‘But the reason I’m going to go back at Villa fans is I can’t believe that a manager who is so successful in the Europa League, take a player, if you’d won the Europa League three or four times (Emery has won it five times) surely you’ll then want to go for the Champions League.

‘Aston Villa will never be Manchester United. I just think he didn’t do well at PSG or Arsenal, and maybe that’s because of egos in the dressing room and that sort of thing.

'But surely he would want that opportunity to manage a giant again. There is a chain in football, whether you like it or not.’

The former Liverpool and England defender eventually apologised for his comments on Saturday, writing on Twitter: 'I’d like to apologise to Aston Villa, the owners & their fans. My language this week was clumsy & wrong.

'I can assure Villa fans it was tongue in cheek but I can understand it’s not come across that way, so apologies. Good luck today UTV!'

Villa have been mocked for this response but look at it from their point of view. The club feel that at every turn, the established order are trying to slow their progress. Consider the financial regulations that favour traditionally wealthy clubs who make money off the pitch, over those who succeed on it.

Imagine the frustration of finishing fourth in the Premier League, winning the Europa League and then having to sell six starters from the final.

Last season Villa finished fourth in the Premier League, won the Europa League and then had to sell six of their starters from the final

Threatening legal action against a pundit may look wild but it does not come from a clear blue sky. Like many of the billionaire class, Sawiris is a tough operator and has taken an increasingly hands-on role at Villa in recent years.

He drove the move to hire Emery in 2022 and he has been more and more involved in transfers. He has forged good, professional relations with some of football’s other key players, including super-agent Jorge Mendes and Chelsea chief Behdad Eghbali. Sawiris ensured Villa received a record fee for Rogers and he was also instrumental in the capture of 18-year-old winger Ibrahim Mbaye from Paris Saint-Germain last summer. His ambition for Villa is limitless.

For seasons now, Villa have operated in what Sawiris may feel is an arbitrary financial straitjacket. Now he has to listen to ex-players with significant influence telling the world that Villa can never satisfy Emery’s ambition.

Carragher is probably guilty of nothing more than expressing an opinion, however crudely he may have done so. But if Sawiris is fed up of various voices and organisations trying to put Villa back in their box, then who can blame him?

Former Manchester United and England striker Wayne Rooney may have already fallen foul of a 'little-known' ITV rule, despite not yet having entered the I'm a Celeb jungle ahead of this year's flagship Ant and Dec show.

Given Rooney's reputation as one of the biggest names in the sporting world, he is expected to be among the show's highest-ever-paid campmates. But if getting off to a good start was part of his plan, he may already have broken a rule.

The former Liverpool and Manchester United star has ranked his top five in order.

The 41-year-old will have to adhere to a number of protocols before entering the jungle, including a psychological evaluation, as well as informing I'm A Celeb bosses about whether there are any trials he would not be able to complete on medical grounds.

Unfortunately for the Red Devils' legend, he cannot rule himself out of underwater trials, despite having admitted he has a phobia of large fish. Meanwhile, he has probably broken protocol which states that contestants cannot seek advice from those who have been on the show before.

#1316. MCT1-dependent mitochondrial lactate import sustains cardiac metabolism

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Nature (2026) Cite this article

The heart possesses a dynamic capacity to oxidize a variety of fuels, including glucose and lactate, to meet its energetic demands under diverse dietary, exertion and injury stressors1. Oxidation of carbohydrate substrates is thought to converge on the cytosolic generation of pyruvate, which is transported by the mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC) for entry into the tricarboxylic acid cycle2. Here we find that glucose-derived carbon is oxidized in mouse myocardium even when the MPC is genetically ablated. Using genetic and pharmacological tools, we demonstrate that lactate monocarboxylate transporter 1 (MCT1, encoded by Slc16a1) is required for the oxidation of glucose carbon by MPC-deficient myocardium. We further observe that MCT1, traditionally localized to the plasma membrane, also resides in the inner mitochondrial membrane of mouse and human cardiomyocytes. Together with matrix-localized LDHB, MCT1 enables mitochondrial lactate conversion to pyruvate and NADH, directly fueling the electron transport chain. Loss of MCT1 impairs lactate oxidation, disrupts metabolic flexibility and accelerates the development of heart failure with increased mortality after hyperactivation of the neurohormonal axis or ischemia–reperfusion injury. Thus, the existence of a parallel lactate-based pathway for carbohydrate oxidation can sustain cardiac energetics and maintain myocardial structure and function under diverse stress conditions.

The oxidation of carbon fuels within the mitochondria is responsible for more than 95% of human ATP production1,3. Dietary carbohydrates supply energy beginning with glycolysis, producing pyruvate that is either reduced to lactate in the cytosol by lactate dehydrogenase (LDH), which also regenerates NAD+, or is imported into the mitochondria for oxidation by the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle4. Circulating lactate turnover exceeds that of glucose in mammalian physiology5,6, establishing lactate production as the dominant mode of cytosolic NAD+ regeneration. Lactate has the same oxidation state as glucose, is a major circulating oxidative fuel source in both fasted and fed mammalian physiology, and is consumed primarily by the heart, skeletal muscle and kidney7,8,9.

Conventional models posit that lactate oxidation starts with the generation of cytosolic pyruvate by LDH, which is subsequently imported into the mitochondria by the obligate heterodimeric mitochondrial pyruvate carrier (MPC, encoded by Mpc1 and Mpc2)2,10. This arrangement leads to competition between LDH and glycolytic enzymes for NAD+, restricting flux through these pathways when metabolic demand is high (Fig. 1a). However, the heart can oxidize both lactate and glucose simultaneously in response to energetic demand11,12,13, suggesting that there might be distinct routes for pyruvate and lactate oxidation14,15.

Here we reconcile the conflict between lactate, glucose and pyruvate oxidation by demonstrating that MCT1, which is canonically on the plasma membrane, is also present on the inner mitochondrial membrane (IMM) of cardiomyocytes. MCT1 is necessary for the uptake and oxidation of lactate, providing metabolic redundancy that sustains cardiac energetics. Genetic ablation of MCT1 abolishes mitochondrial lactate oxidation, disrupts adaptation to neurohormonal, hemodynamic or ischemic stress and accelerates the development of heart failure with enhanced mortality.

To test the prevailing model of lactate oxidation in heart, we utilized our previously described tamoxifen-inducible cardiac-specific Mpc1-knockout mice (Mpc1fl/fl; αMHCMerCreMer+/−, hereafter Mpc1iCKO) to quantify the extent to which the oxidation of glucose and lactate in the myocardium requires the MPC16. We implanted jugular vein catheters into 4 week post-tamoxifen injection (wpi) Mpc1iCKO mice and Mpc1fl/fl littermate controls with normal cardiac function and subsequently infused awake mice with [U-13C]glucose or [U-13C]lactate to reach stable serum enrichment (Extended Data Fig. 1a). Hearts and serum were then collected for isotopic labelling analysis of metabolites by liquid chromatography–mass spectrometry (LC–MS) (Fig. 1b). Similar to prior reports, we observed a rapid appearance of [1,2,3-13C]lactate in serum upon [U-13C]glucose infusion and labelled glucose with [U-13C]lactate infusion, reflecting high rates of interconversion between these metabolites6 (Extended Data Fig. 1b,c). There was no difference in total serum isotopic enrichment and endogenous rates of glucose and lactate appearance between Mpc1fl/fl and Mpc1iCKO mice (Extended Data Fig. 1b–e). We anticipated that the contribution of glucose to TCA cycle metabolites and thus cardiac ATP production would decrease in Mpc1iCKO mice. Unexpectedly, we observed that the glucose carbon contribution to lactate, pyruvate and TCA cycle metabolites increased in Mpc1iCKO mice compared with controls, a finding also reported by others17,18 (Fig. 1c). 13C labelling in the M+1 and M+2 isotopomers of representative TCA metabolites succinate and malate from Mpc1iCKO hearts was increased, but no changes in M+3 isotopomer labelling were seen, indicating enhanced glucose contribution through acetyl-CoA entry to the TCA cycle19 (Extended Data Fig. 1f,g). The contribution of lactate carbon to TCA cycle metabolites trended lower in Mpc1iCKO hearts but was not significantly different for any individual metabolite (Fig. 1d and Extended Data Fig. 1h,i). Using a linear algebra-based approach6, our combined glucose and lactate infusion data showed that Mpc1iCKO hearts used the same total amount of carbohydrate-sourced fuel to supply the TCA cycle, but that it was paradoxically shifted towards glucose in MPC1-deficient hearts (Extended Data Fig. 1j). We performed additional infusions of other major cardiac fuels (palmitate, oleate and 3-hydroxybutyrate) to determine whether Mpc1iCKO mice displayed systemic alterations in cardiac fuel choice that may have confounded our glucose and lactate tracing results (Extended Data Fig. 1k–m). However, the contributions of these fuels to the cardiac TCA cycle were not statistically different from controls, suggesting that heart glucose metabolism is resilient to loss of the MPC in the short term.

Our data from young Mpc1iCKO mice suggests the presence of an MPC-independent mitochondrial import pathway for glucose and lactate carbons. To better understand the cardiomyocyte-intrinsic metabolism of glucose and lactate, we used primary cultured adult cardiomyocytes (ACMs). Control ACMs were competent to oxidize glucose as assessed by 13C incorporation into TCA cycle metabolites (Fig. 1e). However, when unlabelled lactate was added to standard lactate-free ACM culture medium (DMEM) containing [U-13C]glucose, labelling from glucose was attenuated, suggesting a strong preference for lactate over glucose oxidation (Fig. 1e). Lactate consumption was not affected by loss of MPC1 as ACMs from Mpc1iCKO and Mpc1fl/fl mice metabolized lactate into TCA metabolites equivalently (Extended Data Fig. 2a).

Mpc1iCKO mice develop heart failure16,17,20,21 and we investigated whether changes in glucose and lactate oxidation were now present. Mpc1iCKO mice at 16–20 wpi exhibited reduced left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) and hypertrophy (Fig. 1f,g). To successfully introduce stable isotopes into these mice with heart failure, we adopted our protocol to employ a tail vein catheter infusion administered under anaesthesia. Oxidation of glucose and lactate carbon was significantly reduced in failing Mpc1iCKO hearts, despite similar pyruvate and lactate labelling indicating that carbohydrate uptake was not altered (Fig. 1h,i and Extended Data Fig. 2b–f). Total cardiac glycogen was unchanged (Extended Data Fig. 2g). The observed reduction in the oxidation of infused lactate in failing Mpc1iCKO hearts support the hypothesis that there is an MPC1-independent path for lactate oxidation that supports cardiac function.

To identity a potential alternative mitochondrial transporter of lactate, we conducted immunoblot analysis of purified mitochondria from myocardium and observed expression of the lactate transporter MCT1 (encoded by Slc16a1) in the mitochondrial fraction of healthy and failing Mpc1iCKO hearts (Fig. 1j and Extended Data Fig. 2h,i). MCT1 has previously been reported in mitochondria from cardiac tissue22,23. Analysis of published single-nuclei RNA-sequencing data from human hearts showed that SLC16A1 transcripts are predominantly expressed in cardiomyocytes24 (Extended Data Fig. 2j). Notably, MCT1 expression was increased in the mitochondria of young healthy Mpc1iCKO hearts but not failing hearts (Extended Data Fig. 2i,k,l). The existence of mitochondrial lactate import and metabolism has been proposed for decades, but its physiological relevance and mechanistic basis remain actively contested within the field25,26.

To test whether MCT1 can provide an alternative mechanism for carbohydrate carbon entry and oxidation in mitochondria, we repeated our [U-13C]glucose tracing in young, healthy Mpc1iCKO mice cotreated with AZD3965 (AZD), a potent MCT1 inhibitor with selectivity over MCT227. AZD treatment in control mice had no effect on the oxidation of glucose carbon as measured by TCA cycle metabolite labelling (Fig. 2a and Extended Data Fig. 3a–e). However, when AZD was administered to Mpc1iCKO mice, glucose labelling of TCA cycle substrates was ablated. Although MCT1 may have a role in the transport of lactate across both the plasma membrane and IMM, our tracing data support an essential mitochondrial role, as glucose carbon uptake is not dependent on MCT1 activity. Overall, our data suggest functional redundancy between MCT1 and the MPC for the uptake of three-carbon equivalents into the mitochondria.

To further explore the role of MCT1 as a mitochondrial lactate transporter, we developed a tamoxifen-inducible, cardiac-specific Mct1 knockout mouse: Mct1fl/fl; αMHCMerCreMer+/− (hereafter Mct1iCKO). We validated knockout by PCR and MCT1 immunoblots from whole-heart and mitochondrial preparations (Fig. 2b,c and Extended Data Fig. 3f). Across genotypes, a larger fraction of MCT1 signal was associated with mitochondria than MCT2 or MCT4 (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 3f–h). When comparing Mpc1iCKO, Mct1iCKO and control hearts from young mice, we observed an increase in cytosolic and total MCT1, MCT4 and LHDB protein expression in Mpc1iCKO hearts, suggesting a compensatory lactate metabolism axis (Extended Data Fig. 3f,h,i). No significant changes in the expression of these proteins or MPC1 and MCT2 were observed in Mct1iCKO hearts (Extended Data Fig. 3f–j).

We incubated ACMs from Mct1fl/fl (control) and Mct1iCKO mice with [U-13C]lactate to test whether cytosolic uptake of lactate is lost without MCT1. The rate of cytosolic uptake of lactate and production of labelled pyruvate was unaffected by loss of MCT1, suggesting that the observed oxidative phenotypes were unlikely to be the result of changes in cytosolic import (Fig. 2d,e). At steady state, lactate contributed robustly to citrate (M+2) labelling in control ACMs, but this was sharply reduced in Mct1iCKO ACMs. The overall lactate labelling fraction was also reduced, but this was owing to a sharp increase in the total levels of lactate present (Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). To further investigate whether changes in mitochondrial uptake and oxidation of lactate were dependent on MCT1 and independent of its known roles on the plasma membrane, we treated isolated ACMs with saponin to selectively permeabilize the plasma membrane28 (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d). Although plasma membrane integrity was disrupted, mitochondria membrane potential was maintained and cytochrome c was not released (Extended Data Fig. 4d–g). Upon incubation with [U-13C]lactate, we observed robust oxidation in Mct1fl/fl ACMs, as evidenced by TCA cycle labelling that was attenuated in Mct1iCKO cells and upon treatment with AZD3965 (Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 4h,i).

We infused awake Mct1iCKO mice with [U-13C]glucose or [U-13C]lactate to determine whether MCT1 was necessary for the oxidation of lactate in vivo. Serum glucose and lactate metabolic parameters were not different by genotype (Extended Data Fig. 5a–d). In Mct1iCKO hearts, the entry of lactate carbon into TCA metabolites was significantly reduced, whereas labelling from glucose was unchanged (Fig. 2g,h and Extended Data Fig. 5a,b,e–h). Of note, loss of MCT1 did not alter tissue lactate or pyruvate enrichment, indicating that the observed TCA cycle defects were not due to a loss of plasma membrane lactate transport. Oxidation of 3-hydroxybutyrate was also not affected (Extended Data Fig. 5i). To isolate the effects of MCT1 on lactate oxidation alone, we used an ex vivo perfused heart model (Langendorff) with a non-recirculating solution to prevent isotopic exchange between substrates. We cannulated hearts and perfused them with a working buffer containing the major cardiac energy substrates (glucose, lactate, pyruvate and bovine serum albumin (BSA)-conjugated fatty acids)11 (Fig. 2i). Final heart rate was unchanged between Mct1iCKO and control mice (Fig. 2j and Extended Data Fig. 5j). We traced lactate utilization by replacing the unlabelled lactate with [U-13C]lactate (Fig. 2k). Loss of MCT1 prevented nearly all lactate oxidation, but had no effect on lactate enrichment within the tissue. In a second perfusion experiment, we observed that oxidation of [U-13C]glucose was increased in Mct1iCKO hearts, presumably compensating for the loss of lactate oxidation (Fig. 2l).

Paralleling our observations in mouse samples, we detected MCT1 in purified mitochondrial preparations obtained from myocardium of human donors and patients with heart failure (Fig. 3a). To confirm the identity of MCT1 within human mitochondria, we immunoprecipitated MCT1 from purified cardiac mitochondria followed by proteomic analysis. MCT1 peptides were identified together with a high representation of mitochondrial proteins, but not plasma membrane markers, supporting the existence of a mitochondrial MCT1 fraction (Extended Data Fig. 6a–d and Supplementary Table 3). To provide additional evidence of MCT1 and LDHB localization within the mitochondria, we performed proteinase K protection assays using purified mouse and human cardiac mitochondria. In isotonic buffer, intact membranes protect the IMM, intermembrane space and matrix proteins from proteinase K, whereas outer mitochondrial membrane (OMM) proteins are digested. Hypotonic buffer disrupts the OMM, exposing OMM, intermembrane space and some IMM proteins. Detergent (Triton X-100) solubilizes all membranes and denatures protein, rendering all mitochondrial proteins sensitive to proteinase K. Mitochondria from mouse myocardium or isolated cardiomyocytes subjected to these conditions displayed an MCT1 protection pattern resembling that of an IMM protein (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 6e,f). Across preparations, MCT1 was relatively resistant to proteinase K in isotonic buffer, unlike OMM proteins such as TOM20. In these preparations, we also observed a protected LDHB band that showed similar digestion patterns to citrate synthase, a matrix protein. Similar protection patterns were observed in mitochondria from a human cell line, failing human hearts and non-failing human donor hearts (Fig. 3c and Extended Data Fig. 6g,h). Samples from human hearts showed higher variability and more overall degradation due to sample handling differences including freeze–thaw cycles.
