a, Schematic of patient-specific RCC assembloid generation. CA9+ and CA9− cells, CAFs and TII cells were isolated from pretreatment RCC tissues, reconstituted at patient-matched ratios and cultured on a shaker for 7 days. Histopathology, mutational profiles, cellular composition and transcriptomic profiles of assembloids were compared with those of the corresponding parental tumours. Assembloids were then treated with anti-PD-1, and in vitro responses were compared with each patient’s clinical outcome to ICI therapy. b, Schematic workflow for the establishment and maintenance of RCC-derived cultures. For tumour cells, dissociated single-cell suspensions were separated into CA9+ and CA9− populations, each embedded in Matrigel to generate and maintain CA9+ and CA9− organoids, respectively. CAFs were isolated as adherent spindle-shaped cells and expanded in adherent culture. TII cells were maintained and expanded in suspension/adherent culture. c, Representative immunofluorescence images of RCC organoids established without separating CA9+ and CA9− cells at an early stage of culture (top) and maintained in prolonged culture (bottom). Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. d, Representative immunofluorescence images of CA9+ (top) and CA9− (bottom) RCC organoids, with corresponding H&E staining. Scale bars, 100 µm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. e, Oncoplot showing somatic mutations identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. f, Relative fractions of six base substitution types identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. g, Variant-class composition of somatic mutations identified in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations. h, TMB in CA9+ and CA9− cell populations from RCC patients. CR, complete response; NED, no evidence of disease; PD, progressive disease; PR, partial response; SD, stable disease.

a, Representative immunofluorescence images of patient-derived CAFs. Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. b, Gating strategy for the analysis of CAFs. c, Flow cytometry plots of primary CAFs from RCC tissues (top) and cultured CAFs (bottom). Three technical replicates were analysed per group (n = 3). d, Heatmaps showing the relative expression of representative myCAF, iCAF and apCAF marker genes in primary and cultured CAFs derived from six RCC patients, as assessed by RT–qPCR. Three technical replicates were analysed per group (n = 3). e, Pearson correlation analysis of gene expression profiles between primary and cultured CAFs for each patient shown in panel d. Statistics: unpaired two-tailed t-test (c); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c).

a, Representative immunofluorescence images of patient-derived TII cells. Scale bars, 100 μm. The experiments were repeated three times with similar results. b, Gating strategy for the analysis of immune cell populations. c, Flow cytometry plots of primary TII cells from RCC tissues (top) and cultured TII cells (bottom). Three biologically independent samples were analysed per group (n = 3). Statistics: two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (c); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c).

a, Gating strategy used for the analysis of RCC assembloid viability over time. b, Flow cytometry plots showing the proportion of live cells in RCC assembloids from six patients at days 0, 3, 5 and 7 following assembloid formation. Live cells were identified as FVD506-negative cells. c, Quantification of the proportion of live cells in RCC assembloids from six patients at days 0, 3, 5 and 7 following assembloid formation. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed for each time point (n = 3). d, Oncoplot showing the mutational status of a curated panel of genes frequently mutated in RCC, identified by whole-exome sequencing of parental tumours (P-1 to P-6). e, Hierarchical clustering based on TMB, base substitution patterns and variant-class composition. f, TMB in parental tumours and RCC assembloids. g, Relative fractions of six base substitution types in parental tumours and RCC assembloids. h, Variant-class composition of parental tumours and RCC assembloids. i, Proportions of CA9+ and CA9− cells in patient-specific RCC assembloids. j–l, Transcriptomic similarity between parental tumours and RCC assembloids across all 36 parental tumour–assembloid combinations from six patients. Similarity was assessed using HVGs (j), patient DEGs (k) and tumour signatures (l). Detailed methods for these analyses are provided in the Methods. m, Heatmap showing mean expression of representative RCC tumour-cell marker genes in tumour cells from RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. n, Heatmap showing mean expression of representative CAF subtype marker genes in CAFs from RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. o, Heatmap showing mean expression of representative immune cell subtype marker genes in immune cells from RCC assembloids and matched parental tumours across six patient pairs. Data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c,i). A, RCC assembloids; T, parental tumours.

a, Anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids following depletion of stem-like CD8+ T cells. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 μm. b, Experimental design for mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Tumour cells and CAFs from either responders or non-responders were reconstituted with TII cells from either responders or non-responders, as indicated, generating four combinatorial RCC assembloid groups. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days and analysed by flow cytometry. c, Experimental design for combinatorial RCC assembloids. RCC assembloids were generated by selectively removing specific cell populations and cultured for 7 days. These assembloids were used to assess T cell stemness and anti-PD-1 responses. d, Experimental scheme illustrating lineage-tracing analysis of stem-like and non-stem-like CD8+ T cells in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Stem-like (SLAMF6+) and non-stem-like (SLAMF6−) CD8+ T cells were sorted based on SLAMF6 expression and labelled with CellTrace CFSE or CellTrace Blue, respectively, prior to reconstitution into RCC assembloids. e, Flow cytometry gating strategy used for sorting stem-like (SLAMF6+) and non-stem-like (SLAMF6−) CD8+ T cells for lineage-tracing analysis in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. f, Representative flow cytometry plots and quantification of lineage-tracing analysis in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). g, Schematic illustration of three proposed hypotheses for tumour–CAF–CD8+ T cell interactions in maintaining stem-like T cells. Experimental conditions and corresponding results are shown in Fig. 2f–i. h, Schematic workflow for identifying CAF-derived factors involved in stem-like T cell maintenance. CAFs were isolated from RCC assembloids, and comparative transcriptome analysis along with secreted factor profiling was performed to identify candidate genes, which were subsequently validated in functional assays. i, Transcriptomes of control CAFs and CAFs reconstituted with patient-matched tumour cells from responders were compared. Differential expression analysis identified 586 genes upregulated in the reconstituted CAFs (P < 0.05), of which 245 were highly expressed (average expression > 2). Limiting this set to genes encoding secreted proteins further narrowed the list to seven final candidates. j, Schematic diagram to assess the effect of INHBA KD in CAFs from responders on anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids. CAFs were transduced with INHBA shRNA lentiviruses, reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells and cultured for 7 days, followed by anti-PD-1 response analysis. k, Schematic diagram to assess the effects of stem-like CD8+ T cell supplementation in RCC assembloids from responders reconstituted with INHBA KD CAFs. l, Representative fluorescence image showing microinjection of CellTrace CFSE-labelled stem-like CD8+ T cells into RCC assembloids. Scale bar, 100 μm. m, Anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids from responders reconstituted with INHBA KD CAFs following stem-like CD8+ T cell supplementation, with or without activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 μm. n, Proportion of stem-like T cells in RCC assembloids from responders reconstituted with INHBA KD CAFs following stem-like CD8+ T cell supplementation, with or without activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). o, Schematic workflow for identifying tumour cell–derived factors that induce INHBA expression in CAFs. Tumour cells were isolated from RCC assembloids of responders after 7 days of culture. Transcriptomic analysis identified genes expressed in tumour cells (expression level > 0.4), filtered for those positively correlated with INHBA expression in CAFs and predicted to have tumour–CAF communication potential. Candidate genes were subsequently validated in functional assays. p, Experimental strategy to identify tumour-derived ligands that drive activin A (INHBA) expression in CAFs. Bulk RNA-seq of responder cells (CA9+ and CA9−) yielded 9,141 genes with detectable expression. Using NicheNet’s ligand-to-target matrix, we ranked ligands and retained those with positive regulatory potential for INHBA (687 genes), then intersected across samples to obtain 205 ligands with consistent positive potential. Candidate ligands were next evaluated for tumour–CAF signalling using CellChat on the tumour/CAF transcriptomes, which highlighted 14 tumour-to-CAF signalling families; filtering to ligands participating in these pathways produced 37 candidates with tumour–CAF communication potential. q, The 37 candidate ligands expressed in responder tumour cells, grouped by signalling family. r, Schematic diagram to assess the effect of WNT2B KD in tumour cells from responders on anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids. Tumour cells were transduced with WNT2B shRNA lentiviruses, reconstituted with CAFs and TII cells and cultured for 7 days, followed by anti-PD-1 response analysis. s, Schematic workflow for comparative transcriptomic analysis of tumour cells and CAFs from responders and non-responders to investigate mechanisms underlying the anti-PD-1 resistance in non-responders. t, Heatmap showing expression of canonical marker genes for CAF subtypes, analysed by RNA-seq. u, Experimental design of mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Tumour cells and TII cells from responders were reconstituted with CAFs from non-responders, and vice versa, to generate mix-and-match RCC assembloids. These assembloids were cultured for 7 days and subsequently analysed for gene expression and anti-PD-1 responses. v, Relative expression of INHBA in CAFs from mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). w, Anti-PD-1 responses in mix-and-match RCC assembloids. Four biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 12). Scale bars, 100 μm. x, Schematic diagram to assess the effect of LRP6 expression in CAFs from non-responders in RCC assembloids. CAFs were transduced with lentivirus containing LRP6 cDNA, reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells and cultured for 7 days, followed by gene expression and anti-PD-1 response analysis. y, Anti-PD-1 responses in RCC assembloids from non-responders reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells in the absence of CAFs following activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per assembloid (n = 9). Scale bars, 100 μm. z, Proportion of stem-like T cells in RCC assembloids from non-responders reconstituted with tumour cells and TII cells in the absence of CAFs following activin A treatment. Three biologically independent assembloids were analysed per group (n = 3). Statistics: unpaired two-tailed t-test (a,w,z), two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (m,y), one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s multiple-comparison test (n) or two-tailed nested t-test (v); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (a,f,m,n,v,w,y,z). Ctrl, control; αPD1, anti-PD-1.

a, Experimental design for assessing anti-PD-1 responses in humanized mice. WNT2B KD tumour cells from a responder (P-1) or INHBA-expressing CAFs from a non-responder (P-2) were reconstituted with patient-matched CAFs or tumour cells, respectively, and orthotopically transplanted into NSG mice, followed by PBMC infusion and IgG or anti-PD-1 treatment. b, Gating strategy for PBMCs from humanized mice. c, Flow cytometry plots showing human immune cells in PBMCs from humanized mice from a responder (P-1) and a non-responder (P-2). hCD45+ cells were analysed for hCD3+ T cells, hCD19+ B cells, hCD14+ monocytes, hCD4+ T cells and hCD8+ T cells. Five mice were analysed per group (n = 5). d,j, Representative H&E and immunofluorescence images of parental tumours and tumours from humanized mice from a responder (P-1, d) and a non-responder (P-2, j), with quantification of CD45+ and CD8+ cell infiltration (top) and the proportion of CD8+ cells among infiltrating immune cells (bottom). Four biologically independent samples were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per sample (n = 12). e,k, Proportion of CD8+ T cells among infiltrating immune cells. Four mice were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per mouse (n = 12). f,l, Relative expression of WNT2B and INHBA in tumours containing control or WNT2B KD tumour cells (f) and control or INHBA-expressing CAFs (l). Three mice were analysed per group (n = 3). g,m, Representative H&E images of responder-derived tumours (P-1, g) and non-responder-derived tumours (P-2, m) in humanized mice shown in Fig. 4m. Tumour area (mm²) was measured in five H&E-stained sections at 1-mm intervals per kidney, with the mean representing one biological replicate. Four mice were analysed per group (n = 4). Scale bars, 100 μm. h, Gating strategy for tumour-infiltrating human immune cells from xenotransplanted tumours. i,n, Proportion of stem-like T cells in humanized mice from a responder (P-1, i) and a non-responder (P-2, n). Three mice were analysed per group (n = 3). o, Experimental design for assessing anti-PD-1 responses in ALI organoids. Responder organoids (P-5, left) were treated with IWR-1 and non-responder organoids (P-3, right) with recombinant activin A, followed by IgG or anti-PD-1 treatment. p,s, Representative H&E and immunofluorescence images of parental tumours and ALI organoids derived from a responder (P-5, p) and a non-responder (P-3, s), with quantification of CD45+ and CD8+ cell infiltration (top) and the proportion of CD8+ cells among infiltrating immune cells (bottom). Four biologically independent samples were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per sample (n = 12). Scale bars, 100 μm. q,t, Proportion of CD8+ cells among infiltrating immune cells. Four biologically independent organoids were analysed per group, with three sections analysed per organoid (n = 12). r,u, Relative expression of WNT2B and INHBA in ALI organoids treated with control or IWR-1 (r) and control or recombinant activin A (u). Three biologically independent organoids were analysed per group (n = 3). Statistics: unpaired two-tailed t-test (d–f,i–l,n,p–u) or two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (g,m); data show the mean ± s.e.m. (c–g,i–n,p–u).

a, UMAP plots of scRNA-seq data from pretreatment RCC tissues of six patients (P-1, P-4, P-5, P-6: responders; P-2, P-3: non-responders). b, Dot plots showing the expression of selected marker genes for each cluster. c, Feature plots of representative marker genes used to define each cell type. d, Violin plots showing the proportions of major cell types in RCC tumour tissues from responders (R, n = 4) and non-responders (NR, n = 2). e, Feature plots showing the expression patterns of WNT genes in tumour cell clusters. f, Violin plots of representative marker genes for myCAFs, iCAFs and apCAFs, stratified by INHBAhigh and INHBAlow CAFs from RCC patients (n = 6). g, Violin plot showing INHBA expression levels in CAFs from individual patients (n = 6). Statistics: two-tailed Welch’s t-test (d) or two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (g). For box plots (f,g), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range.

a, Schematic workflow for scRNA-seq of pretreatment tumour tissues from responders (R1, R2, R3, R4, R5 and R6) and non-responders (NR1 and NR2). b, UMAP plots showing major cell populations identified in RCC patients (n = 8). c, Dot plots showing the expression of selected marker genes for each cluster. d, Bar graph showing the relative proportions of cell types in individual patients. e, UMAP plot (left) and violin plot (right) showing WNT2B expression levels in tumour cells from individual patients. f, Feature plots showing the expression patterns of WNT ligand genes in tumour cell clusters. g, Correlation of average CAF gene expression profiles between responders and non-responders. h, Dot plot showing expression of canonical marker genes for CAF subtypes. i, UMAP plots of CAFs from responders (R) and non-responders (NR). j, Proportion of INHBAhigh CAFs in responders and non-responders. k, Violin plots of representative marker genes for myCAFs, iCAFs and apCAFs, stratified by INHBAhigh and INHBAlow CAFs from RCC patients (n = 8). l, Violin plots showing expression of INHBA and LRP6 in CAFs from RCC patients (n = 8) stratified by INHBA expression status. m, Violin plot showing INHBA expression levels in CAFs from individual patients. n, Violin plots showing expression of LRP6 in CAF subclusters. o, GSEA of INHBAhigh versus INHBAlow CAFs showing enrichment of the WNT signalling pathway in INHBAhigh CAFs. p, Violin plots showing expression of the stem-like T cell signature in CD8+ T cells from responders (R, n = 6) and non-responders (NR, n = 2). q, Schematic workflow of spatial transcriptomic analysis of pretreatment RCC tissues from one responder and one non-responder, using publicly available Visium datasets obtained from GEO (GSM641570540 for the responder; GSM592403841 for the non-responder). r,s, Left, spatial maps of transcriptional clusters overlaid on tissue sections from the responder (r) and the non-responder (s). Right, corresponding spatial feature plots showing cell type–specific gene signatures. t, Representative spatial transcriptomic maps from a responder and a non-responder, showing WNT2B+ tumour spots, TCF7+ CD8+ T cell spots, LRP6+ myCAF spots and LRP6+INHBA+ myCAF spots, alongside H&E-stained images and spatial feature plots of cell type marker genes. u, Violin plots showing WNT2B expression in tumour spots from responders and non-responders. v, Box plots quantifying the number of CAF spots adjacent to WNT2B+ tumour spots in RCC patients (n = 2). w, Box plots depicting spatial relationships between WNT2B+ tumour spots, CAF spots and TCF7+ CD8+ T cell spots in RCC patients (n = 2). x, GSEA of CAF spots adjacent to WNT2B+ tumour spots between one responder and one non-responder. y, Schematic workflow of spatial transcriptomic analysis performed on pretreatment RCC tissues from an independent cohort of six patients (three responders, three non-responders) using GeoMx DSP. z, Representative GeoMx DSP ROI images from responders (case1–3) and non-responders (case4–6). Tumour and myCAF regions were identified by PanCK (green) and αSMA (red) staining, respectively. ROIs designated for sequencing of tumour and myCAF regions are indicated. aa–gg, Comparative transcriptomic analyses of tumour and myCAF regions in responders versus non-responders. aa, Linear similarity in tumour (PanCK+) regions. bb, PCC heatmap showing transcriptional similarities of tumours across individual responders and non-responders. cc, WNT2B expression in tumour (PanCK+) regions in RCC patients (n = 6). dd, Linear similarity of myCAF (αSMA+) profiles between responders and non-responders. ee, PCC heatmap showing transcriptional similarities of myCAFs across individual responders and non-responders. ff, INHBA expression in myCAF (αSMA+) regions in RCC patients (n = 6). gg, Pathway enrichment analysis of myCAFs based on upregulated DEGs in responders, demonstrating enrichment of WNT signalling–associated pathways. Statistics: two-way ANOVA followed by Sidak’s multiple-comparison test (d), two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (e,l–n,p,v–x), unpaired two-tailed t-test (cc,ff) or one-sided Fisher’s exact test, with FDR correction for multiple comparisons (gg). For box plots (k–n,p,v,w), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range. Data show the mean ± s.e.m. (cc,ff).

a, Schematic overview of the analytical strategy across four solid tumour types (gastric, lung, ovarian and prostate cancers) using TCGA bulk RNA-seq datasets. Tumours with enriched WNT expression were selected, and target patient subsets were subsequently stratified into two groups based on T cell stemness signatures, INHBA expression and LRP6 expression. b, Identification of target patient subsets in gastric cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer and prostate cancer. Patient ranking plots are shown based on WNT expression, hot tumour signatures and CAF-associated signatures. c, Proportion of target patients identified in each cancer type from TCGA bulk RNA-seq datasets. Target patients were defined based on enrichment of WNT expression together with hot tumour and CAF-associated signatures. d, Left, heatmaps showing T cell stemness signature, INHBA expression, LRP6 expression and WNT expression in target patients identified by k-means clustering. Right, box plots comparing T cell stemness signature, INHBA expression, LRP6 expression and WNT expression between the two identified patient groups (gastric cancer, n = 169; lung cancer, n = 622; ovarian cancer, n = 127; prostate cancer, n = 108). e, Schematic overview of the analytical strategy used to analyse bulk RNA-seq datasets from ICI-treated patients across three solid tumour types (gastric, lung and ovarian cancers). Patient subsets exhibiting enriched WNT expression were identified, and correlations among immunotherapy responses, INHBA/LRP6/T cell stemness signature and WNT expression were subsequently analysed. f, Identification of target patient subsets in gastric, lung and ovarian cancers. Patient ranking plots are shown based on WNT expression. g, Transcriptomic analyses of ICI-treated cohorts from gastric, lung and ovarian cancers. Top, heatmaps showing integrated joint scores for INHBA/LRP6/T cell stemness signature and WNT expression in the analysed patient cohorts. Bottom, box plots comparing responders (R) and non-responders (NR) with respect to integrated INHBA/LRP6/T cell stemness scores and WNT expression (gastric cancer, n = 70; lung cancer, n = 83; ovarian cancer, n = 38). h, Schematic overview of the analytical strategy used to analyse scRNA-seq datasets across four solid tumour types (gastric, lung, ovarian and prostate cancers). Patient subsets harbouring WNT-expressing tumours were identified, and cell-type-specific expression of WNT, INHBA and LRP6, as well as correlations among the proportion of stem-like CD8+ T cells, the proportion of INHBA+LRP6+ CAFs and tumoural WNT expression, were subsequently analysed. Patients lacking detectable CAF or CD8+ T cell populations were excluded from downstream analyses. i, UMAP plots showing major cell populations identified by scRNA-seq in gastric cancer, lung cancer, ovarian cancer and prostate cancer. j, Heatmaps showing representative marker gene expression patterns across major cell populations within each cancer type. k, Feature plots (left) and patient ranking plots (right) showing tumour WNT expression in individual patients from each cancer type. Patients harbouring WNT-expressing tumour cells were selected for downstream analyses. l, Heatmaps showing the proportions of INHBA- and LRP6-expressing cells across major cell populations within each cancer type. m, Top, heatmaps showing the proportions of stem-like CD8+ T cells and INHBA+ and/or LRP6+ CAFs across target patient subsets identified by clustering analyses. Two patient groups were stratified based on the proportions of stem-like CD8+ T cells and INHBA+ and/or LRP6+ CAFs. Bottom, box plots comparing the proportions of stem-like CD8+ T cells and INHBA+/LRP6+ CAFs between the two identified patient groups (gastric cancer, n = 19; lung cancer, n = 27; ovarian cancer, n = 8; prostate cancer, n = 9). n, Left, heatmaps showing WNT expression in tumour cells across target patient subsets identified by clustering analyses. Right, box plots comparing tumoural WNT expression between the two identified patient groups (gastric cancer, n = 19; lung cancer, n = 27; ovarian cancer, n = 8; prostate cancer, n = 9). Statistics: two-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test (d,m,n) or two-tailed Welch’s t-test for WNT expression and the one-sided Wilcoxon rank-sum test for integrated joint scores (g). For box plots (d,g,m,n), centre lines indicate medians, box limits indicate the interquartile range and whiskers extend to the most extreme data points within 1.5 × the interquartile range.

In this study, we identified dynamic interactions among tumour cells, CAFs and CD8+ T cells that determine tumour responses to ICIs in human RCC. CAF-derived activin A promotes the maintenance and expansion of the TCF1+ stem-like CD8+ T cell pool in inflamed tumours, thereby establishing a responding hot tumour state. In this setting, tumour-derived WNT2B induces activin A production in LRP6-positive CAFs, which in turn sustains CD8+ T cell stemness and drives expansion of the stem-like T cell pool. By contrast, when activin A expression is minimal or absent in inflamed settings due to the presence of tumour-adjacent LRP6-deficient CAFs, it fails to sustain CD8+ T cell stemness, resulting in non-responding hot tumours and resistance to anti-PD-1 therapy.

#1307. One Everton Man Higher Than Dewsbury-Hall: Players Rated and Slated vs Newcastle

Everton secured a 1-0 victory over Newcastle at St James' Park, making it two wins against the Magpies in just four days.

It was a bright first half for Everton, and David Moyes will be wondering how his side weren't in front heading into half-time.

The ball fell to Thierno Barry from just a few yards out in the first half, but he failed to connect properly with the ball after taking a wild swing at it.

Later in the half, another big chance fell Everton's way. A smart run and pass from Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall helped find Harrison Armstrong, but he somehow missed the target with his first-time effort.

Shortly after the break, Everton found themselves in front. A smart set-piece routine allowed Dewsbury-Hall to find Tyrique George with a superb pass. He fired an effort at goal that went through goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek, allowing Barry to tap home the opener.

It was a deserved opener for the Toffees after their missed chances in the first half, and Newcastle could have no complaints as Everton went 1-0 up.

Always an interesting game for Jordan Pickford, being a Sunderland lad. The Newcastle supporters certainly let him know!

Pickford was anonymous in the first half, which is everything Moyes would have wanted, with Newcastle barely testing the goalkeeper.

After another fairly quiet half, Pickford, one of the best goalkeepers in the Premier League right now, made a crucial save in the final seconds with his feet, denying Yoane Wissa from close range.

Jake O’Brien hasn’t been given too many opportunities by David Moyes so far this season, but he came in at right-back vs Newcastle. The Republic of Ireland international kept Harvey Barnes quiet, while he was also a threat in both boxes aerially.

It was a comfortable start to the evening for both centre-backs in the first half, with Newcastle showing minimal threat. As per usual, James Tarkowski was winning everything.

When paired with Jarrad Branthwaite, Everton are more often than not an incredibly solid side at the back. The Newcastle game was no different.

It’s a similar story for Jarrad Branthwaite as it was for Tarkowski. He was incredibly solid at the back, and his inclusion allowed Everton to play a high line due to his pace. Newcastle tried to get in behind regularly, particularly in the first half, but Branthwaite was always there to snuff it out.

Further reports about Grealish have come to light after he was left out of Everton's squad to face Newcastle.

Vitalii Mykolenko has had plenty of criticism since his move to Everton, but he’s looked a different player this season. That was no different against Newcastle, with another solid display. Never anything outlandish or crazy in terms of performance levels, but solid.

James Garner, as he always does, showed plenty of energy in the middle of the park for Everton. Sitting in front of the back four allowed his midfield partners the freedom to get forward.

Sometimes Garner’s influence on the team isn’t too noticeable due to it being mostly off-the-ball work, but he was a key figure in the middle nonetheless.

Harrison Armstrong showed plenty of energy in the first half, and he should have got himself on the scoresheet. One of the best chances of the game fell to him after some good work by Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall, but his right-footed strike from around 12 yards out was comfortably wide, when he should have scored.

Perhaps one of the surprise inclusions, starting at right-wing like he did against Chelsea. The German showed plenty of energy on the right-hand side in the first half, causing Lewis Hall problems.

Rohl was clearly used as an outlet for Everton, using his pace to get in behind in transition. He also tracked back well to help the Toffees out defensively.

Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall was playing in his usual advanced midfield role. In the first half, Dewsbury-Hall was finding himself in lots of space in between the lines, and was undoubtedly Everton’s most creative threat.

That showed as Everton opened the scoring, finding George with a superb pass before his shot was palmed away and tapped in by Barry.

Overall, a faultless performance from the former Chelsea midfielder. He was everywhere, and played a crucial role in the goal.

It was a quiet first half for Tyrique George, who struggled to get himself involved.

Shortly after the break, however, George made a clever run from a set-piece to fire at Lukas Hornicek, with the goalkeeper spilling it before Barry fired home.

Fairly quiet overall, but didn't do an awful lot wrong.

Thierno Barry had an excellent chance to open the scoring for Everton in the first half, taking a wild swipe at the ball from close range, but he failed to connect properly.

Barry did make up for his missed chance, though, scoring the opening goal of the game as he tapped home from close range just after the break.

Barry struggled to get involved in the game outside of his opportunities in front of goal, but ultimately, scored the winner for the Toffees.

Further reports about Grealish have come to light after he was left out of Everton's squad to face Newcastle.

Although Dewsbury-Hall was the best performer on the pitch, David Moyes has to be given his flowers.

The Everton manager has taken a lot of criticism in recent weeks, but he answered those critics with a fantastic 1-0 away victory.

Moyes made some bold decisions to take Hayden Hackney and Tyler Dibling out of the team, while also starting Merlin Rohl at right wing.

When you make decisions like that, they have to work out, and no one can question Moyes for the decisions he made against Newcastle.

The team looked incredibly balanced and fully deserved their victory.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

Barry is a nice guy but a dreadful footballer, I know we have to wait till January to bring in an alternative, but, in the interim, shortly we can fine a deputy from within the squad. Dibling may not be a striker, but he might be able to control the ball when played up to him, but I'm open to suggestions.

#1306. Serie A official line-ups: Atalanta vs. Parma

Giorgio Scalvini returns to the Atalanta defence, while Giovanni Fabbian replaces the injured Adrián Bernabé in the Parma midfield and Simone Lontani partners El Bilal Touré up front.

It kicks off at 20:45 CET [19:45 GMT] at the New Balance Arena, with Valerio Crezzini refereeing.

Atalanta are 11th on 11 points and haven’t won at home since beating Venezia on 12 October. Their last home game was a chaotic 4-4 draw with Frosinone, and they followed it with a 2-2 draw at Fiorentina on Thursday, when Charles De Ketelaere and Nicola Zalewski scored. Maurizio Sarri has warned his side not to underestimate Parma, pointing to their low block and threat on the counter.

Parma are in the bottom three on five points in Serie A so far. Alberto Gilardino is still looking for his first win since replacing Carlos Cuesta at the end of September, and Wednesday’s 0-0 draw with Udinese was his first point after three straight defeats. Bernabé had a penalty saved in that game.

Atalanta’s injury crisis means Sarri has called up only 19 players. The latest additions to the list are Gianluca Gaetano with a medium-grade adductor strain in his right thigh. And Thomas Kristensen, who suffered a low-grade hamstring strain in his left thigh.

Both were hurt in Florence and will return after the international break. Raoul Bellanova, Gianluca Scamacca, Giacomo Raspadori, Sead Kolašinac, Franck Kessié, Isak Hien, Odilon Kossounou and Pompei are also out. Giorgio Scalvini is back in the squad.

Adrián Bernabé misses out for Parma after feeling a muscle problem in his left leg in training on Sunday. Elphege is back in the squad after appendicitis surgery.

Atalanta: Carnesecchi; Zappacosta, Obrić, Scalvini, Bernasconi; Pašalić, Ederson; Rowe, De Ketelaere, Zalewski; Krstović. Coach: Sarri

Parma: Daffara; Drobnič, Troilo, Delprato; Britschgi, Fabbian, Sierro, Keita, Valeri; Lontani, Touré. Coach: Gilardino
